whyNot.A: A CRL (Certificate Revocation List) lists revoked certificates and is not submitted to request a new one.
whyNot.B: OCSP (Online Certificate Status Protocol, written OSCP here) checks whether a certificate is revoked and is not used to request a certificate.
whyNot.C: A PFX (Personal Information Exchange) file is a container format for a certificate and private key, not a request for a new certificate.
whyNot.E: The CA (Certificate Authority) is the entity that issues certificates, so it is what receives the request rather than what is submitted.

230.why: DNSSEC (Domain Name System Security Extensions) adds RRSIG (Resource Record Signature) records so DNS (Domain Name System) answers, including MX (Mail Exchanger) and address lookups, can be authenticated.

whyNot.B: SFTP (Secure File Transfer Protocol) transfers files securely and does not answer or authenticate DNS (Domain Name System) lookups.
whyNot.C: nslookup is a client tool for querying DNS (Domain Name System) and is not a server that performs authenticated responses.
whyNot.D: dig (Domain Information Groper) is a client query tool and not a publicly hosted service that signs or authenticates records.
whyNot.E: LDAPS (Lightweight Directory Access Protocol over Secure Sockets Layer) secures directory queries and has nothing to do with DNS (Domain Name System) record lookups.

231.why: Sending a PIN (Personal Identification Number) to a phone is out-of-band verification, which proves the person holds a second, separate channel that an attacker is unlikely to control.

whyNot.A: A single security question is often guessable or findable from public information, so it is weak for password recovery.
whyNot.C: CAPTCHA (Completely Automated Public Turing test to tell Computers and Humans Apart) slows automated attacks but is not a password recovery method.
whyNot.D: A different e-mail address can itself be compromised or protected by a weak password, so it is less trustworthy than a separate device.

232.why: Change management procedures require review, testing, and approval of how multiple changes interact before release, which would catch a flaw that only appears when two updates are combined.

whyNot.B: Job rotation moves staff between duties to detect fraud and reduce collusion, and does not test how code changes interact.
whyNot.C: Incident response management handles events after they occur and does not prevent a flawed release from shipping.
whyNot.D: Least privilege access controls limit user permissions and do not address the combined effect of two software updates.

233.why: Opening messages in plain text prevents HTML (Hypertext Markup Language) and script content from rendering, so accidentally opening a malicious email does not run its embedded exploit.

whyNot.A: Host-based firewalls filter network traffic and do not stop malicious content from being rendered by the email client.
whyNot.C: End-point protection relies largely on known signatures and behavior, and may not stop a zero-day exploit that has never been seen.
whyNot.D: Spam filters for one sender only block that sender and do not stop the same attack from arriving from a different address.

234.why: The key credits OCSP (Online Certificate Status Protocol) for checking certificate validity, but it requires a live connection to a responder, so it would not work during an extended internet outage.

whyNot.A: A recovery agent restores encrypted data when keys are lost and does not check whether certificates are valid.
whyNot.C: The key rejects CRL (Certificate Revocation List), but a locally cached CRL can be checked offline, which is why keyDoubt prefers it.
whyNot.D: Key escrow stores copies of private keys for recovery and does not verify certificate validity.

234.keyDoubt: C. A CRL (Certificate Revocation List) can be downloaded and cached locally, so validity can still be checked during an internet outage, while OCSP (Online Certificate Status Protocol) needs a live responder.

235.why: HMAC (Hash-based Message Authentication Code) provides integrity and authentication without encrypting data, which fits ESP (Encapsulating Security Payload) used with integrity protection only.

whyNot.B: PCBC (Propagating Cipher Block Chaining) is an encryption mode, so it provides confidentiality, which the requirement excludes.
whyNot.C: CBC (Cipher Block Chaining) encrypts data and provides confidentiality, not integrity-only protection.
whyNot.D: GCM (Galois/Counter Mode) provides both encryption and authentication, so it includes confidentiality, which is not wanted here.
whyNot.E: CFB (Cipher Feedback) is an encryption mode that provides confidentiality and no integrity protection on its own.

236.why: Certificates signed by the company's internal CA (Certificate Authority) are trusted by managed internal clients and cost nothing extra, satisfying the HTTPS (Hypertext Transfer Protocol Secure) policy.

whyNot.B: Using a CA (Certificate Authority) signing certificate as a wildcard certificate is improper and exposes the signing key on every server.
whyNot.C: Certificates from a public CA (Certificate Authority) require fees, which violates the no-additional-cost requirement.
whyNot.D: Self-signed certificates are not trusted by clients, cause browser warnings, and are hard to manage across many servers.

237.why: Penetration testing actively exploits vulnerabilities and reports which ones were actually exploited, which suits a system with no uptime requirement or users.

whyNot.A: Peer review is a colleague examination of code or design and does not exploit anything.
whyNot.B: Component testing checks that individual parts function correctly and does not attempt to exploit vulnerabilities.
whyNot.D: Vulnerability testing identifies potential weaknesses without exploiting them, so its report does not show what was actually exploited.

238.why: Creating a new read-only group applies least privilege and role-based access control, giving the intern only the needed access without changing anyone else's permissions.

whyNot.A: Modifying every shared file to read-only would remove write access for the Purchasing staff who need it and is error-prone.
whyNot.C: Removing all permissions would block the intern and all legitimate users from the shared files.
whyNot.D: Adding the intern to the Purchasing group would grant write access, violating the principle of least privilege.

239.why: OS (Operating System) hardening removes unneeded services, applies patches, and tightens settings, which reduces the attack surface of laptops exposed on untrusted wireless networks.

whyNot.A: MAC (Media Access Control) filtering is a network-side control that does not protect laptops on networks the company does not manage, and addresses are easily spoofed.
whyNot.B: Virtualization isolates workloads but does not by itself reduce the exposure of the host laptop to network attacks.
whyNot.D: Application white-listing limits which programs run but does not harden the laptop against network-based attacks.

240.why: The Lessons Learned phase of incident response reviews what went wrong, such as missing tools, and drives process improvements for future incidents.

whyNot.A: Reporting documents and communicates the incident and does not focus on fixing process gaps.
whyNot.B: Preparation is where the gap originated, but reviewing and improving it happens afterward in Lessons Learned.
whyNot.C: Mitigation is the active containment of the incident in progress and not the time for review of process failures.

241.why: A host-based firewall (software firewall on the laptop) blocks unsolicited inbound connections, so another patron on the same coffee shop network cannot directly reach services on Joe's laptop.

whyNot.A: Full-disk encryption protects data at rest if the device is stolen, but does not stop network connections to a running laptop.
whyNot.C: Current antivirus definitions detect known malware but do not block a nearby person from directly connecting to the laptop.
whyNot.D: The latest operating system updates fix vulnerabilities but do not filter or block direct inbound network connections.

242.why: A replay attack captures valid network traffic, such as a transaction, and retransmits it later to repeat the effect. Resending the captured gift card packets repeatedly adds value each time.

whyNot.A: An integer overflow attack makes a numeric value exceed its storage limit, not retransmit captured packets.
whyNot.B: A Smurf attack floods a victim with ICMP (Internet Control Message Protocol) echo replies via spoofed broadcast requests, which is a denial of service, not a transaction replay.
whyNot.D: A buffer overflow attack writes more data than a memory buffer can hold, not resending captured packets.
whyNot.E: A cross-site scripting attack injects malicious scripts into web pages viewed by users, which does not involve resending sniffed packets.

243.why: Federated authentication lets the cloud provider trust the company's identity provider through assertions such as SAML (Security Assertion Markup Language), so users keep internal credentials and the provider never stores their passwords.

whyNot.A: Two-factor authentication adds a second proof of identity but does not prevent the provider from holding copies of passwords.
whyNot.B: Account and password synchronization copies passwords to the provider, which is exactly what the security manager wants to avoid.
whyNot.C: Smartcards with PINs (Personal Identification Numbers) strengthen authentication but do not by themselves keep the provider from receiving or storing credentials.

244.why: The bottleneck is the volume of data replicated to the offsite data center, so reducing data on the storage array before replication reduces what must be transferred and shortens the backup window.

whyNot.A: Network-level deduplication between the sites could cut transfer volume, but it is not the keyed choice here and adds appliance complexity.
whyNot.C: Deduplicating on server storage reduces data stored on the source server, but does not necessarily reduce the replicated backup set.
whyNot.D: Deduplicating on both local and remote servers saves storage at both ends but does not specifically address the replication bottleneck.

244.keyDoubt: A. The bottleneck is replication across the network to the offsite data center, so deduplication at the network level between the two locations directly reduces transferred data.

245.why: A protocol analyzer (packet capture tool) records the actual network traffic, which provides raw evidence proving and validating what the scanning tools reported.

whyNot.A: Logging outbound connections at the firewall shows only connection metadata, not the packet contents needed to validate scan results.
whyNot.C: Network flow data (such as NetFlow) summarizes traffic statistics but lacks the packet detail needed to prove scan findings.
whyNot.D: Debug logging shows what the tools report internally, which is the data to be validated, not independent proof of it.

246.why: Per the keyed answer, the phone and storage cards are examined together as a unit after the removable storage cards have been examined separately, so each source is preserved and evaluated.

whyNot.A: Powering down and removing the battery can alter volatile data and may trigger device lock features, so it is not the proper initial processing step.
whyNot.B: Processing only removable storage first does not describe a complete initial processing approach for the whole mobile device.
whyNot.C: Examining the device first, then storage, then the phone again repeats work and risks altering evidence on the device.

246.keyDoubt: C. This sequence of examining the device, then removable storage, then the phone without storage is closer to recognized mobile forensics guidance, though the key's wording is loosely supported.

247.why: A packet analyzer (protocol analyzer or sniffer) captures and decodes network traffic so an analyst can inspect the contents of the suspicious connections to the call back domain.

whyNot.A: A vulnerability scanner finds weaknesses in systems but does not decode live network traffic.
whyNot.B: NMAP (Network Mapper) discovers hosts and open ports but does not decipher captured traffic contents.
whyNot.C: NETSTAT (network statistics) lists local connections and listening ports but does not show or decode packet contents.

247.keyDoubt: D. A packet analyzer is the tool that actually deciphers network traffic, whereas NETSTAT (network statistics) only lists connections.

248.why: Collision resistance means it should be infeasible to find two different inputs producing the same hash. The keyed wording is garbled, but it points to the strongest test, which is finding any colliding pair.

whyNot.B: Two identical messages always produce the same hash, so finding this proves nothing about collision resistance.
whyNot.C: Finding a common hash for two specific chosen messages is a harder, more constrained target, so it is a weaker practical test than finding any collision.
whyNot.D: Matching a specific message to a random one is a second preimage style search, which is a different property than collision resistance.

248.keyDoubt: C. Finding a common hash between two specific messages is the closest option to a true collision test, since option A as worded describes an impossible case.

249.why: Wireless access points answer broadcast probe requests with their network information even when SSID (Service Set Identifier) broadcast is off. Disabling those responses further hides the network from scanners.

whyNot.A: Upgrading to WPA (Wi-Fi Protected Access) or WPA2 strengthens encryption but does not hide the presence of the network.
whyNot.B: Creating a non-zero length SSID would make the network name visible, not further obscure it.
whyNot.C: Rerouting users to a honeypot (decoy system) is a deception technique and does not hide the wireless network.

250.why: SRTP (Secure Real-time Transport Protocol) adds encryption, authentication, and integrity protection to RTP (Real-time Transport Protocol) media streams, which is how voice traffic is encrypted.

whyNot.A: SSLv3 (Secure Sockets Layer version 3) is a deprecated, insecure protocol and is not designed for encrypting voice media streams.
whyNot.B: VDSL (Very-high-bit-rate Digital Subscriber Line) is a broadband access technology, not an encryption method.
whyNot.D: VoIP (Voice over Internet Protocol) is the voice transport technology itself, not an encryption mechanism.

251.why: LDAP (Lightweight Directory Access Protocol) used for single sign-on verifies a user's credentials against the directory, which is authentication, proving the claimed identity is genuine.

whyNot.A: Application control restricts which programs may run, which is unrelated to verifying users against a directory.
whyNot.B: Data in-transit describes protecting data moving across a network, not the process of verifying user identity.
whyNot.C: Identification is claiming an identity, such as giving a username, while the directory lookup verifying it is authentication.

252.why: A user rights and permission review compares each person's access with their job role, finding excess privileges such as accumulated administrator rights after a merger.

whyNot.A: Time-of-day restrictions limit when accounts can log in but do not correct excessive permissions.
whyNot.B: Change management controls how system changes are approved and documented, not whether user access is appropriate.
whyNot.C: Periodic auditing of user credentials checks credential use and strength, whereas the problem here is excess rights, which the rights review addresses.

253.why: An SLA (Service Level Agreement) defines expected performance and service delivery, so an audit of the partner against it verifies those performance and service delivery metrics are being met.

whyNot.B: Backup performance and testing is a specific operational control that an SLA audit does not primarily verify.
whyNot.C: Data ownership is usually set in contracts or data governance agreements, not verified through SLA (Service Level Agreement) metrics.
whyNot.D: Risk awareness enforcement is a policy and training matter, not what an SLA (Service Level Agreement) audit measures.

254.why: ALE (Annualized Loss Expectancy) is SLE (Single Loss Expectancy) multiplied by ARO (Annualized Rate of Occurrence), giving the expected yearly monetary damage from an exploited vulnerability.

whyNot.B: ARO (Annualized Rate of Occurrence) is only how often an event is expected per year, not a monetary value.
whyNot.C: MTBF (Mean Time Between Failures) measures how long a system typically operates between failures, not monetary damage.
whyNot.D: TCO (Total Cost of Ownership) measures the full lifetime cost of owning an asset, not the damage from an exploit.

255.why: A signature based IDS (Intrusion Detection System) compares activity to a database of known attack patterns, such as a vendor provided list, and alerts on matches.

whyNot.B: Heuristic detection uses rules and algorithms to spot suspicious behavior, not a fixed vendor list of known patterns.
whyNot.C: Anomaly-based detection flags deviations from a learned normal baseline rather than matching a provided list.
whyNot.D: Behavior-based detection watches for abnormal actions over time, not matches against a vendor supplied list.

256.why: Data loss with no break-ins points to insider or user error, so security awareness training teaches employees to handle data properly and reduces accidental or careless disclosure.

whyNot.A: Protected distribution (a physically secured cabling system) guards against wire tapping, not data loss caused by user behavior.
whyNot.B: Adding firewalls blocks external network attacks, but no break-ins occurred, so perimeter filtering will not address the data loss.
whyNot.D: Perimeter barricades stop physical vehicle or intruder access, which is irrelevant since no break-ins have occurred.

257.why: Exterior lighting discourages would-be intruders from approaching because they fear being seen, which makes it a deterrent control rather than one that blocks or detects.

whyNot.B: A compensating control substitutes for another control that cannot be implemented, and lighting here is not replacing anything.
whyNot.C: A detective control identifies an event after or as it occurs, such as logs or alarms, and lighting alone does not detect anything.
whyNot.D: A preventative control physically stops an action, such as a lock or fence, while lighting only discourages the attempt.

258.why: User access reviews periodically compare active accounts and permissions against current employees, so accounts of former staff with VPN (Virtual Private Network) access are found and disabled.

whyNot.A: Time-of-day restrictions limit when accounts can log in, but they do not remove or identify accounts belonging to departed employees.
whyNot.C: Group-based privileges simplify permission assignment, but they do not detect stale accounts that remain active after employees leave.
whyNot.D: Change management policies control how system changes are approved and documented, not the review of user account status.

259.why: An SLA (Service Level Agreement) defines the services, security responsibilities, and performance a cloud provider must deliver, so it is where required administrative and logical controls would be specified.

whyNot.B: An ISA (Interconnection Security Agreement) governs the technical security of connecting two systems, not the provider's overall administrative and logical controls.
whyNot.C: An NDA (Non-Disclosure Agreement) protects confidentiality of shared information but does not specify the provider's required security controls.
whyNot.D: A BPA (Business Process Analysis) examines internal business workflows and does not bind a provider to protect data.

260.why: DAC (Discretionary Access Control) lets the data owner decide who can access a resource and set the access rules, which matches empowering data owners.

whyNot.A: MAC (Mandatory Access Control) uses central labels and clearances set by administrators, so data owners cannot manage the rules.
whyNot.C: RBAC (Role Based Access Control) assigns access by job role defined centrally, not by individual data owners.
whyNot.D: Rule-based access control applies centrally defined rules such as time or location conditions, not owner-managed permissions.

261.why: A man-in-the-middle attack places the attacker between two parties, relaying and possibly altering their communications while each side believes it is talking directly to the other.

whyNot.A: Spear phishing is a targeted deceptive message to trick a victim, not interception and forwarding of live communications.
whyNot.C: URL hijacking (typosquatting) relies on look-alike domain names to catch mistyped addresses, not on intercepting an ongoing exchange.
whyNot.D: Transitive access is a trust relationship where access passes through an intermediate party, and it is not an interception attack.

262.why: SCP (Secure Copy Protocol) runs over SSH (Secure Shell) and FTPS (File Transfer Protocol Secure) adds TLS (Transport Layer Security) to FTP, so both encrypt file transfers.

whyNot.B: TFTP (Trivial File Transfer Protocol) has no authentication or encryption, so it is not secure for external file transfers.
whyNot.C: SNMP (Simple Network Management Protocol) is used for device monitoring and management, not file transfer.
whyNot.D: FTP (File Transfer Protocol) sends credentials and data in clear text, so it is not secure.
whyNot.E: SMTP (Simple Mail Transfer Protocol) transports email and is not a file transfer protocol, and it is unencrypted by default.

263.why: Transitive authentication relies on trust established through another element, here the office location or computer, so authentication succeeds only when the login originates from the trusted office system.

whyNot.A: Dual factor authentication requires two different factor types, but the scenario requires only username and password plus a location restriction.
whyNot.C: Single factor authentication checks only one factor and has no way to reject logins based on where they originate.
whyNot.D: Biometric authentication uses physical traits such as fingerprints, which the scenario does not call for.

263.keyDoubt: A transitive trust is not really a location control; a location-based restriction fits better, and among these options none is clearly correct, so B is the loose best fit.

264.why: A captive portal requires a user to interact with a web page before getting internet access, which an embedded thermostat cannot do, so it associates and gets an address but cannot reach the internet.

whyNot.B: An incorrect encryption algorithm would prevent association with the AP (Access Point), but the thermostat is already associated.
whyNot.C: An incorrect WPA2 (Wi-Fi Protected Access 2) shared key would block association, yet the thermostat associated and received network parameters.
whyNot.D: A full DHCP (Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol) scope would prevent an address lease, but the thermostat received the expected network parameters.

265.why: Rule 3 denies HTTP and HTTPS (Hypertext Transfer Protocol and its Secure variant) web traffic to the blocked sites list, and the wildcard entries can match the partner's website, preventing access.

whyNot.A: Rule 1 blocks SMTP (Simple Mail Transfer Protocol) email traffic, which does not affect browsing a website.
whyNot.B: Rule 2 blocks ping (ICMP, Internet Control Message Protocol), which does not stop web page access.
whyNot.D: Rule 4 would block everything, but it would also stop all other web access, which is not described as happening.

266.why: A polymorphic virus changes its code or binary pattern to evade signature-based detection, which matches malware that alters its pattern to avoid being identified.

whyNot.A: An armored virus uses techniques to hinder analysis and reverse engineering rather than changing its binary pattern on a schedule.
whyNot.B: A logic bomb triggers a malicious action on a specific condition or date, but it does not change its binary pattern to evade detection.
whyNot.D: A Trojan disguises itself as legitimate software to get installed, and does not inherently alter its binary pattern.

266.keyDoubt: C is the best match for pattern changing, though the date and time trigger resembles a logic bomb, so the wording is loose but the key is acceptable.

267.why: Twofish is a symmetric block cipher that uses one shared key for both encryption and decryption, which is what file encryption with a symmetric key requires.

whyNot.A: RSA (Rivest-Shamir-Adleman) is an asymmetric algorithm using a public and private key pair.
whyNot.C: Diffie-Hellman is a key exchange protocol for agreeing on a shared secret, not an algorithm for encrypting files.
whyNot.D: NTLMv2 (NT LAN Manager version 2) is an authentication protocol, not a file encryption cipher.
whyNot.E: RIPEMD (RACE Integrity Primitives Evaluation Message Digest) is a hashing algorithm, which cannot be reversed to decrypt files.

268.why: An SLA (Service Level Agreement) documents what services will be delivered, how and when, and the penalties if the provider fails to meet the agreed levels.

whyNot.A: An MOU (Memorandum of Understanding) states general intent between parties and typically lacks detailed performance terms and penalties.
whyNot.B: An ISA (Interconnection Security Agreement) specifies technical security requirements for connecting systems rather than service penalties.
whyNot.C: A BPA (Business Partnership Agreement) defines the relationship and responsibilities of business partners, not detailed service delivery and penalties.

269.why: Birthday attacks exploit hash collisions, where two different inputs produce the same hash value, so hashed passwords are the most susceptible.

whyNot.B: Digital certificates are signed using hashes, but certificate use is not the most direct target of collision-finding compared with hashed passwords.
whyNot.C: Encryption passwords protect keys or data and are attacked through brute force or dictionary methods, not hash collisions.
whyNot.D: OTP (One Time Passwords) are valid for a single use or short time, so a collision found later gives little advantage.

270.why: The order of volatility collects the most volatile evidence first, such as memory, then network traffic, then disk, because volatile data is lost quickly.

whyNot.B: Chain of custody documents who handled evidence and when, not the sequence in which evidence is collected.
whyNot.C: Recovery procedure restores systems to normal operation after an incident, rather than collecting evidence.
whyNot.D: Incident isolation separates affected systems to contain damage, and it does not define the order of evidence collection.

271.why: PGP (Pretty Good Privacy) encrypts messages for confidentiality and uses digital signatures, which provide non-repudiation because only the sender's private key could have produced the signature.

whyNot.A: Bcrypt is a password hashing function; it cannot encrypt messages for recipients or provide non-repudiation.
whyNot.B: Blowfish is a symmetric cipher that encrypts data but offers no digital signature, so it cannot provide non-repudiation.
whyNot.D: SHA (Secure Hash Algorithm) produces a hash for integrity and does not encrypt messages or prove who sent them.

272.why: The log shows a successful login on local port 23, which is Telnet, a protocol that sends credentials and data in cleartext. Disabling Telnet and enabling SSH (Secure Shell) encrypts the session.

whyNot.A: Port security limits which MAC (Media Access Control) addresses use a switch port and does not encrypt Telnet traffic.
whyNot.C: An AAA (Authentication, Authorization, and Accounting) server centralizes access control but the Telnet session would still travel in cleartext.
whyNot.D: Replacing passwords with RSA (Rivest-Shamir-Adleman) authentication does not fix the cleartext transport that Telnet uses.

273.why: A certificate chain runs from the end-entity certificate through any intermediate CA (Certificate Authority) up to the root CA. The missing link here is the intermediate authority that issued the company certificate.

whyNot.A: A CRL (Certificate Revocation List) reports revoked certificates and is not part of the chain of trust.
whyNot.C: A recovery agent can recover encrypted data keys and is not a certificate chain element.
whyNot.D: The root of trust is the root CA certificate, which the administrator already loaded into the file.

274.why: Full device encryption makes the laptop's drive unreadable without the key or credentials, so data confidentiality is kept even if the device is lost or stolen.

whyNot.A: Remote wipe needs network connectivity to the device, so a thief can keep it offline and still reach the data.
whyNot.C: A BIOS (Basic Input/Output System) password can be bypassed by removing the drive and reading it elsewhere.
whyNot.D: GPS (Global Positioning System) tracking helps locate the laptop but does not protect the data stored on it.

275.why: Deduplication needs a fast hash that is widely supported. SHA (Secure Hash Algorithm) is fast, available on nearly every platform, and has far fewer collision weaknesses than MD5 (Message Digest 5).

whyNot.A: MD5 (Message Digest 5) is fast but has known collision weaknesses, which could make different files appear identical.
whyNot.C: RIPEMD (RACE Integrity Primitives Evaluation Message Digest) is a hash that has much less support across systems than SHA.
whyNot.D: AES (Advanced Encryption Standard) is a symmetric encryption cipher and not a hashing algorithm.

276.why: SFTP (Secure File Transfer Protocol) runs over SSH (Secure Shell) to replace FTP (File Transfer Protocol), and TLS (Transport Layer Security) secures web traffic by replacing plain HTTP (Hypertext Transfer Protocol) with HTTPS.

whyNot.B: TFTP (Trivial File Transfer Protocol) has no encryption or authentication, so it does not replace HTTP securely.
whyNot.C: Telnet transmits everything in cleartext and is not a secure replacement for HTTP (Hypertext Transfer Protocol).
whyNot.D: IPSec (Internet Protocol Security) is a network-layer tunneling suite and not a direct application replacement for HTTP file transfers.

277.why: Avoidance eliminates the risk by ceasing the risky activity. Suspending operations at the unstable facility removes exposure to the political unrest.

whyNot.A: Deterrence discourages threat actors with warnings or controls and does not stop the activity itself.
whyNot.B: Mitigation reduces the likelihood or impact of a risk while operations continue, but here operations are stopped.
whyNot.D: Acceptance means knowingly continuing operations and living with the risk, which is the opposite of suspending them.

278.why: Account lockout disables an account after repeated failed logins, which limits attackers who brute-force credentials to hijack accounts for spam. It is the best listed technical control here.

whyNot.B: Group based privileges assign permissions by group and do not stop compromised accounts from sending spam.
whyNot.C: Least privilege limits access rights, but a compromised account can still send email with normal user permissions.
whyNot.D: Password complexity makes guessing harder but does not stop repeated attempts the way lockout does.

278.keyDoubt: A is the best of the options listed, though the question is loosely worded; no different answer is clearly better.

279.why: PKI (Public Key Infrastructure) lets each user encrypt files with the recipient's public key and decrypt with their own private key, so no credentials or keys need to be exchanged.

whyNot.A: Key escrow stores copies of keys with a third party for recovery and does not let users share encrypted files.
whyNot.B: Digital signatures prove origin and integrity but do not encrypt the file contents.
whyNot.D: Hashing creates a one-way digest for integrity and cannot encrypt data for sharing.

280.why: Digital signatures use the signer's private key, so only that person could have created them. This provides non-repudiation, since the signer cannot credibly deny the action.

whyNot.A: Transitive trust extends trust between domains and does not prove who performed an action.
whyNot.B: Symmetric encryption uses a shared key, so either party could have created the message and nobody can be proven the author.
whyNot.C: Two-factor authentication strengthens login identity but does not create a verifiable record that binds a person to an action.
whyNot.E: One-time passwords improve authentication but do not give proof of origin that prevents denial.

281.why: FIM (File Integrity Monitoring) compares file hashes to a baseline and alerts when files such as website images change unexpectedly, which would reveal Joe's steganography-modified images.

whyNot.A: Digital signatures verify authenticity of signed content but do not detect unauthorized replacement of ordinary website files.
whyNot.C: Access controls matter, but Joe is a website administrator who legitimately has write access to those files.
whyNot.D: Change management is a process that Joe could bypass, and it does not detect unauthorized file changes by itself.
whyNot.E: A stateful inspection firewall filters network connections and does not detect altered files on the server.

282.why: Key stretching repeatedly applies a salted hash to a password to slow brute-force attempts. Algorithms such as PBKDF2 (Password-Based Key Derivation Function 2) and bcrypt do this.

whyNot.A: Collision resistance describes a hash's difficulty of producing two inputs with the same output and is not a repeated-hashing process.
whyNot.B: A rainbow table is a precomputed hash lookup table used to attack passwords, and salting defeats it.
whyNot.D: A brute force attack is an attacker guessing passwords, not a defensive hashing technique.

283.why: SAML (Security Assertion Markup Language) exchanges authentication and authorization assertions between identity providers and service providers across organizations, enabling federated single sign-on.

whyNot.B: Active Directory is a directory service that manages identities inside one organization's domain and is not a federation standard.
whyNot.C: Kerberos is a ticket-based authentication protocol used mainly within a single realm or domain.
whyNot.D: LDAP (Lightweight Directory Access Protocol) queries directory information and does not provide federation across organizations.

284.why: MAC (Media Access Control) spoofing lets an attacker copy the address of an authorized device, which can bypass weak MAC-based exceptions such as those used for devices that cannot do 802.1X.

whyNot.B: Pharming redirects users to fake websites through DNS (Domain Name System) manipulation and does not bypass LAN access control.
whyNot.C: An Xmas attack is a port scan using unusual TCP (Transmission Control Protocol) flags and does not bypass 802.1X.
whyNot.D: ARP (Address Resolution Protocol) poisoning redirects traffic on a LAN after access is already obtained, so it does not get past 802.1X.

285.why: AES (Advanced Encryption Standard) is a symmetric encryption algorithm commonly used by IPSec (Internet Protocol Security) to encrypt VPN (Virtual Private Network) traffic.

whyNot.A: MD5 (Message Digest 5) is a hashing algorithm and does not encrypt data.
whyNot.C: UDP (User Datagram Protocol) is a transport protocol and not an encryption algorithm.
whyNot.D: PKI (Public Key Infrastructure) is a framework for managing certificates and keys, not an encryption algorithm.

286.why: Kerberos uses tickets issued by a Key Distribution Center (KDC) to identify and authenticate users without resending passwords, which is the feature unique among RADIUS (Remote Authentication Dial-In User Service), Diameter, and Kerberos.

whyNot.A: Providing authentication services is common to RADIUS (Remote Authentication Dial-In User Service), Diameter, and Kerberos, so it is not unique to Kerberos.
whyNot.C: Single sign-on (SSO) is not unique to Kerberos, since other federated and directory-based systems also provide single sign-on.

287.why: Humidity controls affect electrostatic discharge (ESD) because low humidity lets static charge build up on people and equipment, while proper humidity levels dissipate it and protect network hardware.

whyNot.A: Fire suppression protects against fire damage and does not influence static charge buildup in a network operations center.
whyNot.B: Environmental monitoring only observes and reports conditions like temperature and humidity, so it does not itself change electrostatic discharge (ESD) risk.

288.why: Header manipulation alters HTTP (Hypertext Transfer Protocol) header fields, such as the Referer value, in intercepted traffic, which matches an attacker inserting a line that sets the referrer URL (Uniform Resource Locator).

whyNot.D: XML (Extensible Markup Language) injection inserts malicious XML content into an application and does not set HTTP (Hypertext Transfer Protocol) referrer headers.

289.why: Blacklisting (a deny list) blocks a known set of unwanted applications while allowing everything else, which fits a requirement to prevent specific known applications from running.

whyNot.A: Whitelisting (an allow list) permits only approved applications and blocks everything else, which is broader than blocking just a known set.

290.why: Storage segmentation in MDM (Mobile Device Management) separates corporate data from personal data in containers, so the company can remotely wipe only its own data without affecting the user's personal data.

whyNot.A: Asset control tracks and inventories devices and does not separate corporate data from personal data.
whyNot.B: Device access control restricts who or what can use the device or resources and does not enable selective removal of company data.
whyNot.C: Storage lock out locks the device or storage after failed attempts and does not partition corporate data for selective removal.

291.why: In STP (Spanning Tree Protocol), the root bridge is elected by the lowest bridge ID (priority plus MAC, Media Access Control, address); with default priorities, the switch with the lowest MAC address wins, even if it is old and slow.

whyNot.A: Acting as a DHCP (Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol) server has no bearing on STP (Spanning Tree Protocol) root bridge election.
whyNot.C: Loop protection features like root guard or BPDU (Bridge Protocol Data Unit) guard prevent unwanted root elections rather than cause them.
whyNot.D: Uplink speed affects path cost calculations but is not a criterion for electing the STP (Spanning Tree Protocol) root bridge.

292.why: DAC (Discretionary Access Control) lets the data owner decide who gets permissions on files, documents, and directories, which is simple and removes central administrative overhead.

whyNot.A: Rule-based access control applies centrally defined rules, such as time or network conditions, and does not let users set permissions.
whyNot.B: RBAC (Role-Based Access Control) assigns permissions by job role through central administration, which adds overhead and does not let users decide.
whyNot.C: MAC (Mandatory Access Control) uses central labels and clearances enforced by the system, which is complex and removes user discretion.

293.why: Minimum complexity and minimum length raise the number of possible password combinations, making brute force attacks take far longer and therefore most effectively improving resistance to them.

whyNot.B: A maximum age limit forces periodic password changes and does not make an individual password harder to brute force.
whyNot.C: A maximum length limit would restrict password strength rather than improve it against brute force attacks.
whyNot.E: A minimum age limit prevents rapid password changes and does not increase the difficulty of brute force attacks.
whyNot.F: A re-use limit stops people from recycling old passwords and does not make a new password harder to brute force.

294.why: Application whitelisting, enforced with operating system controls, permits only approved software to run and blocks everything else, which meets a policy of no exceptions for unapproved applications.

whyNot.A: Antivirus detects known malicious or pirated software but does not block all unapproved applications from running.
whyNot.B: A firewall blocking executable downloads cannot stop software arriving through other means such as USB (Universal Serial Bus) drives or approved channels.
whyNot.D: Removing administrator rights limits installation but does not prevent unapproved portable applications from running.

295.why: The question asks for authorized commands and central logging of administrator activity, which is the job of TACACS+ (Terminal Access Controller Access-Control System Plus), providing authentication, command authorization, and accounting. The keyed LDAP (Lightweight Directory Access Protocol) distinguished name only handles directory lookup.

whyNot.A: An LDAP (Lightweight Directory Access Protocol) server entry only handles authentication and cannot restrict commands or log them.
whyNot.C: A SYSLOG (System Logging) server provides central logging but does not authenticate users or authorize commands.
whyNot.D: TACACS+ (Terminal Access Controller Access-Control System Plus) provides command authorization and accounting, but it is misspelled here; however it is not the keyed answer.

296.why: Steganography hides data inside a media file such as an MPEG (Moving Picture Experts Group) video, changing the file's hash value while the content looks and plays the same.

whyNot.A: Cryptography protects data confidentiality through encryption and would not by itself explain a changed hash on media that looks unchanged.
whyNot.B: Time of check/time of use (TOCTOU) is a race condition between validating and using a resource and does not alter a file's hash invisibly.
whyNot.C: A man in the middle (MITM) attack intercepts communications and does not specifically explain hidden changes inside a media file.
whyNot.D: Covert timing is a covert channel that signals information through timing and does not modify the file's contents.

297.why: PFS (Perfect Forward Secrecy) generates a unique session key for each exchange, so compromising one session key cannot decrypt earlier or later captured communications.

whyNot.A: Asymmetric encryption uses public and private key pairs and does not by itself guarantee that each session uses an independent key.
whyNot.B: Out-of-band key exchange delivers keys through a separate channel but does not ensure that one compromised key is isolated from other sessions.
whyNot.D: Secure key escrow stores copies of keys with a trusted party for recovery and does not protect other sessions from a compromised key.

298.why: The rule must match the shared HTTP (Hypertext Transfer Protocol) scheme, .info domain, and specific URI (Uniform Resource Identifier) path and query, while keeping false positives low; the keyed option is the most specific pattern, blocking only that path and query on .info domains.

whyNot.A: Blocking every http .info URL (Uniform Resource Locator) is too broad and would block many legitimate sites, causing false positives.
whyNot.B: Dropping the specific website.info domain misses phishing URLs on other .info domains that share the same URI (Uniform Resource Identifier).
whyNot.C: Redirecting rather than blocking still lets users reach a modified page, and the pattern contains typos that would not match correctly.

299.why: Denying all IP (Internet Protocol) traffic from the single attacking host 192.168.1.10/32 stops this attack and any further attacks from that address, while leaving every other source unaffected and minimizing service interruption.

whyNot.A: Denying TCP (Transmission Control Protocol) from any source to the server would block all legitimate users and cause a service outage.
whyNot.B: Denying UDP (User Datagram Protocol) from a whole /24 subnet is too broad and targets the wrong protocol and wrong destination network.
whyNot.D: Denying only TCP (Transmission Control Protocol) from the attacker to one server still allows the attacker to use other protocols or reach other hosts.

300.why: Least privilege gives users only the permissions they need, so without administrative rights they cannot install untested applications on their systems.

whyNot.A: Job rotation moves staff between roles to reduce fraud and does not restrict software installation.
whyNot.C: Account lockout disables accounts after repeated failed logins and does not control which applications users can install.
whyNot.D: Antivirus detects known malware but does not stop users from installing untested yet non-malicious applications.

301.why: Using a similar wireless configuration of a nearby network describes an evil twin or rogue access point attack, where a competing signal interferes with legitimate wireless traffic and disrupts clients. Interference is the main effect.

whyNot.A: Overloading a target's memory allocation describes a buffer overflow, which corrupts memory rather than interfering with network signals.
whyNot.B: Using a previously unknown flaw describes a zero-day exploit, which is not about interference with network traffic.
whyNot.D: Inundating a target with SYN (Synchronize) requests is a SYN flood Denial of Service (DoS) attack, which exhausts connection resources instead of causing interference.

301.keyDoubt: D: Interference is a stretch for any option, but a SYN (Synchronize) flood is the only one that clearly impedes network traffic as a Denial of Service (DoS) attack, so it is the likelier intended answer.

302.why: Diffie-Hellman is a key exchange algorithm that lets two parties derive a shared secret over an insecure channel, so the data files can then be encrypted with that key.

whyNot.A: DES (Data Encryption Standard) is a symmetric cipher for encrypting data, not an algorithm for exchanging keys.
whyNot.B: Blowfish is a symmetric block cipher used to encrypt data, not to exchange keys.
whyNot.C: DSA (Digital Signature Algorithm) is used to create and verify digital signatures, not to exchange keys.
whyNot.E: 3DES (Triple Data Encryption Standard) is a symmetric cipher for encrypting data, not for key exchange.

303.why: Training on the use of social networking teaches employees that posts may be publicly visible and can have professional repercussions, which is exactly what Ann missed.

whyNot.A: Data labeling and disposal training covers classifying and destroying data, not appropriate public posting behavior.
whyNot.C: P2P (Peer-to-Peer) networking training covers file sharing risks, not posting comments on a website.
whyNot.D: Role-based training covers duties specific to a job function, not general public online conduct.

304.why: A vulnerability scan identifies weaknesses such as missing security patches on services and desktops, which matches the audit finding.

whyNot.A: Network mapping discovers hosts and topology but does not check for missing patches.
whyNot.C: A port scan finds open ports and services but does not determine whether patches are missing.
whyNot.D: Protocol analysis inspects captured network traffic and does not assess patch levels on hosts.

305.why: SHA (Secure Hash Algorithm), specifically SHA-256 or stronger, is the modern, secure hash used when generating certificate requests and signatures for x.509 certificates.

whyNot.A: RC4 (Rivest Cipher 4) is a stream cipher, not a hashing algorithm, and is deprecated.
whyNot.B: MD5 (Message Digest 5) is broken by collision attacks and should not be used for certificates.
whyNot.C: HMAC (Hash-based Message Authentication Code) is a keyed construction for message authentication, not the hash used in certificate requests.

306.why: Encrypting each field as it is written to disk protects data at-rest, meaning data stored on persistent media.

whyNot.A: Data in-transit is data moving across a network, which is not what writing fields to disk describes.
whyNot.B: Data in-use is data being actively processed in memory or by the CPU (Central Processing Unit), not stored on disk.
whyNot.C: Embedded is not a standard data state; it refers to embedded systems, not the state of encrypted data.

307.why: SAML (Security Assertion Markup Language) lets an application authenticate a user based on an assertion from an identity provider in a web domain, enabling federated single sign-on.

whyNot.A: TACACS+ (Terminal Access Controller Access-Control System Plus) authenticates and authorizes administrative access to network devices, not web application logins.
whyNot.B: RADIUS (Remote Authentication Dial-In User Service) centralizes network access authentication, not web domain federation for applications.
whyNot.C: Kerberos is a ticket-based authentication protocol for internal network domains, not for receiving credentials from a web domain.

308.why: A protocol analyzer, or packet sniffer, captures and displays packet contents such as IPv4 (Internet Protocol version 4) data on a network segment.

whyNot.A: A proxy relays and filters client requests but is not used to view packet data on a segment.
whyNot.C: A switch forwards frames between ports and does not by itself display packet data.
whyNot.D: A firewall filters traffic by rules and logs events but is not a tool for viewing full packet data.

309.why: Changing antenna placement and adjusting power level controls limit how far the WiFi signal propagates beyond the building, reducing exposure to war driving from outside the fence line.

whyNot.A: A honeynet is a decoy network for studying attackers and does not stop the signal from reaching the parking area.
whyNot.B: Reducing the beacon rate makes the network slower to discover but does not stop determined war drivers or limit signal range.
whyNot.C: Adding false SSIDs (Service Set Identifiers) only adds noise and does not limit signal reach or protect the real network.
whyNot.F: A warning banner is a legal notice and does not technically prevent signal capture or war driving.

310.why: DLP (Data Loss Prevention) alerts show sensitive data leaving the environment, and log analysis can reveal unauthorized remote access and transfers, together helping confirm exfiltration.

whyNot.A: NAC (Network Access Control) controls which devices can connect but does not confirm whether data was exfiltrated.
whyNot.D: FIM (File Integrity Monitoring) detects changes to files, but exfiltration copies data without necessarily modifying it.
whyNot.E: Host firewall rules restrict traffic as preventive controls and do not provide evidence of past exfiltration.

311.why: Placing VoIP (Voice over Internet Protocol) traffic in its own VLAN (Virtual Local Area Network) isolates it from data traffic and allows QoS (Quality of Service) prioritization, improving performance and availability.

whyNot.B: Upgrading edge switches does not fix the saturated core switches or isolate voice traffic from data traffic.
whyNot.C: Physically separating the networks would be costly and is unnecessary when a VLAN (Virtual Local Area Network) provides logical separation.
whyNot.D: Flood guards protect against denial of service floods and do not address congestion or voice traffic isolation.

312.why: RDP (Remote Desktop Protocol) can be tunneled inside TLS (Transport Layer Security) over an allowed port such as 443, letting the administrator reach the server despite the closed default port.

whyNot.B: MPLS (Multiprotocol Label Switching) is a carrier WAN (Wide Area Network) routing technology, not a tunneling method for RDP (Remote Desktop Protocol) on another port.
whyNot.C: SCP (Secure Copy Protocol) transfers files over SSH (Secure Shell) and does not carry remote desktop sessions.
whyNot.D: SSH (Secure Shell) could tunnel RDP (Remote Desktop Protocol), but it would typically use port 22, which is likely also blocked, making TLS the better fit.

312.keyDoubt: D: SSH (Secure Shell) port forwarding is the classic way to tunnel RDP (Remote Desktop Protocol) to a different port, whereas TLS (Transport Layer Security) alone is not a tunneling method.

313.why: TACACS+ (Terminal Access Controller Access-Control System Plus) provides command-level authorization, letting administrators control which commands users may run on network infrastructure devices.

whyNot.A: LDAP (Lightweight Directory Access Protocol) is a directory service for storing and querying identities, not for per-command device authorization.
whyNot.B: Kerberos provides ticket-based authentication and does not authorize individual device commands.
whyNot.C: SAML (Security Assertion Markup Language) handles federated web authentication and does not control commands on network devices.

314.why: Active Directory federation lets the company vouch for users through trust between identity providers, so the SSL-inspecting IDS (Intrusion Detection System) never sees the user's credentials or decryption keys.

whyNot.A: OATH (Open Authentication) one-time passwords with attestation still involve credentials passing through the inspected path, and the model does not address certificate-based mutual authentication.
whyNot.C: Smartcards storing x.509 keys signed by a global CA (Certificate Authority) still perform the mutual TLS handshake through the SSL-inspecting IDS (Intrusion Detection System).
whyNot.D: A third-party SAML (Security Assertion Markup Language) service adds an external party and does not by itself keep credentials away from the inspecting IDS (Intrusion Detection System).

315.why: Validating the feasibility of a new requirement and its security impact is part of the system analysis phase of the SDLC (Software Development Life Cycle), where requirements are defined and assessed.

whyNot.A: The system integration phase combines completed components and tests them together, rather than evaluating new requirements.
whyNot.C: The system design phase defines architecture after requirements are settled, not feasibility of a newly introduced requirement.
whyNot.D: The system development phase is where code is written, which comes after requirements have been analyzed and approved.

316.why: Little evidence was available from the role-based authentication system, which points to a log failure: the logging and auditing needed to attribute actions and support the investigation was missing or inadequate.

whyNot.A: Job rotation moves employees between duties to detect fraud; it does not explain missing authentication evidence.
whyNot.C: Lack of training concerns employee knowledge and is not what left the investigation without usable records.
whyNot.D: An insider threat describes who may have caused the exfiltration, not the gap in logging that hampered the investigation.

317.why: A VPN (Virtual Private Network) concentrator gives the vendor an encrypted, authenticated channel, and limiting the vendor to desktop sharing on the PACS (Physical Access Control System) balances security with quick remote support.

whyNot.A: Permitting outbound internet access for a legacy-operating-system PACS (Physical Access Control System) exposes an unpatchable device to the internet.
whyNot.B: An onsite visit is secure but slow, so it fails the urgency and efficiency requirement.
whyNot.D: Remotely connecting from the administrator's PC through a web conference exposes that workstation and bypasses controlled, authenticated vendor access.

318.why: The operating system is the foundation that every application and service runs on, so it must be restored first before other software can function.

whyNot.A: Communications software depends on a working operating system, so it is restored after the operating system.
whyNot.C: Weekly summary reports to management are not time-critical and can wait until core systems are recovered.
whyNot.D: Financial and production software needs a running operating system first, so it is recovered afterward.

319.why: The key lists session hijacking and cross-site scripting, but locally shared objects (Flash cookies) are the textbook way to persist tracking data outside normal browser privacy settings.

whyNot.A: SQL (Structured Query Language) injection attacks the database through unsanitized input and does not bypass browser privacy settings.
whyNot.B: Session hijacking steals an active session token but does not defeat the browser's privacy settings.
whyNot.E: LDAP (Lightweight Directory Access Protocol) injection manipulates directory queries on the server and does not affect browser privacy settings.

319.keyDoubt: D and C: locally shared objects (Flash cookies) persist outside browser privacy controls, and cross-site scripting runs script in the browser, whereas session hijacking steals tokens rather than bypassing privacy settings.

320.why: Input validation must be enforced on the application server, a trusted layer the attacker cannot alter, so malicious input is rejected before it reaches the database.

whyNot.A: Client-side validation can be bypassed by an attacker who modifies requests or disables scripts, so it is only a convenience.
whyNot.B: Database stored procedures validate too late, after the application has accepted the input, and do not replace server-side validation.
whyNot.D: HTTPS (Hypertext Transfer Protocol Secure) encrypts traffic in transit but does not check whether the submitted data is malicious.

321.why: Egress filtering and monitoring can reveal compromised internal hosts communicating with known botnet command-and-control sources, which lets administrators block and detect that outbound traffic.

whyNot.A: Egress traffic is not inherently more important than ingress traffic; both need filtering as part of defense in depth.
whyNot.B: Egress filtering is a security control and is not used to rebalance inbound and outbound traffic volumes.
whyNot.D: Preventing DDoS (Distributed Denial of Service) attacks from external networks is an ingress concern, not the purpose of egress filtering.

322.why: A minimum password age stops users from changing their password repeatedly within a short period, which curtails the many same-day password changes.

whyNot.A: Password reuse describes the problem of reusing old passwords and is not a control that limits how often changes occur.
whyNot.B: Password complexity sets character requirements and does not limit how frequently a password can be changed.
whyNot.C: Password history blocks reuse of old passwords, but users can still change passwords many times a day.

323.why: SAML (Security Assertion Markup Language) authentication provides federated single sign-on with centrally managed identity, and MFA (Multifactor Authentication) requires more than one proof of identity before cloud data is accessed.

whyNot.A: Block level encryption protects data at rest but does not control or strengthen who is able to access the cloud data.
whyNot.C: Transport encryption protects data in transit but does not strengthen authentication to the cloud service.
whyNot.E: Predefined challenge questions are weak, guessable knowledge factors and do not meaningfully enhance access security.
whyNot.F: Hashing provides integrity checking and cannot control access to data stored in the cloud.

whyNot.A: Network latency would cause slow or intermittent connections rather than a consistent failure to reach the workstation.

whyNot.D: A compromised workstation visiting malware sites would not by itself explain why User1 cannot reach the workstation.
whyNot.E: A host firewall blocking RDP (Remote Desktop Protocol) would be shown as denied connections, which is not what the keyed answer indicates.

325.why: Separation of duties requires that no single person controls an entire process, so requesting, approving, and implementing firewall rules should be split among different people.

whyNot.A: Discretionary access control lets owners assign permissions and does not split request, approval, and implementation roles.
whyNot.C: Least privilege limits the rights a person has, but does not by itself divide one process among several people.
whyNot.D: Mandatory access control uses system-enforced labels and clearances and does not address one person holding every step of the change process.

326.why: A DMZ (Demilitarized Zone) is a network segment between the internet and the internal network that hosts externally facing servers while still allowing controlled internal access.

whyNot.A: NAC (Network Access Control) checks the posture of devices connecting to the network and does not create a zone for public-facing servers.
whyNot.B: A VLAN (Virtual Local Area Network) logically separates traffic but does not by itself provide a protected zone for external services.
whyNot.D: A subnet divides an address range and does not provide the filtered boundary needed for externally exposed servers.

327.why: Users can download but not upload, which indicates the FTP (File Transfer Protocol) service account lacks write permission, so an ACL (Access Control List) granting write access to user directories fixes it.

whyNot.B: An SELinux (Security-Enhanced Linux) Boolean could also block uploads, but nothing in the scenario suggests SELinux is enforcing, and plain permissions are the likelier cause.
whyNot.C: Passive mode affects how data connections are established, and downloads already work, so it would not selectively block uploads.
whyNot.D: PAM (Pluggable Authentication Modules) pass-through affects authentication, which already works since users can log in and download.

328.why: Remote syslog sends log entries to a separate protected server in real time, so an attacker who alters local logs cannot erase the copies and further tampering becomes detectable.

whyNot.A: Verbose logging records more detail locally, but an attacker with access can still alter or delete those local files.
whyNot.B: Changing permissions on a user's home directory does not protect the system log files from alteration.
whyNot.D: Setting the bash_history file to read only protects only command history and does not protect system logs or detect tampering.

329.why: Firmware version control stops consoles from running modified or downgraded firmware, and automatic updates keep every console on the current, trusted firmware.

whyNot.B: Manual software upgrades depend on customers acting, so modified consoles can simply stay on old, vulnerable versions.
whyNot.C: Vulnerability scanning finds known weaknesses but does not stop customers from modifying their own consoles.
whyNot.E: Network segmentation separates the manufacturer's network traffic and does not prevent physical or software modification of consoles.
whyNot.F: Application firewalls filter traffic to applications and do not prevent customers from modifying console firmware or software.

330.why: Separation of duties prevents the same people who administer the databases from also auditing their changes and backup logs, so oversight is independent.

whyNot.A: Time of day restrictions limit when accounts can log in and do not separate administration from auditing.
whyNot.B: Least privilege limits the rights each person has, but does not specifically stop one person from both administering and auditing.
whyNot.C: RBAC (Role-Based Access Control) assigns permissions by role, but it would not fix the conflict unless duties are separated into different roles and people.

331.why: Black box testing means the tester has no prior knowledge of the target's software or network architecture, which matches a contractor given no information.

whyNot.B: White box testing gives the tester full knowledge of the architecture and source, the opposite of this scenario.
whyNot.C: Passive reconnaissance is an information-gathering technique, not a penetration test type defined by how much knowledge the tester has.
whyNot.D: A vulnerability scan is an automated search for known weaknesses and does not describe a penetration test's knowledge level.

332.why: A CRL (Certificate Revocation List) publishes revoked certificates, so every browser can check it and reject the hijacked certificate without configuring each machine individually.

whyNot.A: SSL (Secure Sockets Layer) is an encryption protocol and does not revoke or invalidate a compromised certificate.
whyNot.C: PKI (Public Key Infrastructure) is the overall certificate framework, not the specific revocation mechanism needed here.
whyNot.D: An ACL (Access Control List) filters access to resources and has no ability to distrust a certificate across browsers.

333.why: The keyed answer is port scanning, but a network tap only observes traffic and sends no probes, so port scanning is a questionable fit.

whyNot.A: Compliance scanning checks configurations against a policy baseline and does not describe passively watching tapped traffic.
whyNot.B: Credentialed scanning logs in to hosts with valid accounts, which a network tap does not do.
whyNot.C: Passive vulnerability scanning is the better fit for tapped traffic, but it is not the keyed answer.

333.keyDoubt: C. A network tap only copies and observes traffic without sending probes, which is passive vulnerability scanning, whereas port scanning actively sends packets to hosts.

334.why: BitLocker provides full drive encryption on Windows, and it relies on a TPM (Trusted Platform Module) enabled in the BIOS (Basic Input/Output System) to securely store the keys.

whyNot.A: EFS (Encrypting File System) encrypts individual files and folders, not the full drive as the regulation requires.
whyNot.C: VT-x (Intel Virtualization Technology) supports virtual machines and has nothing to do with drive encryption.
whyNot.E: DFS (Distributed File System) organizes and replicates shared folders and does not encrypt any data.

335.why: Motion detectors sense movement in the datacenter and raise an alert, so they detect equipment theft when someone removes or moves gear.

whyNot.A: Biometrics authenticate people at an entry point and do not detect equipment being removed.
whyNot.B: Cameras record activity and mainly help investigation afterward, rather than detecting theft as it happens.
whyNot.D: Mantraps are physical entry controls that prevent tailgating and do not detect equipment removal.

336.why: Reconnaissance is the information-gathering phase of a penetration test, and using public Internet databases to learn about a target is passive reconnaissance (also called open source intelligence).

whyNot.B: Initial exploitation means actively compromising a system, not just looking up public information.
whyNot.C: Pivoting means using an already compromised host to reach other systems on the network.
whyNot.D: Vulnerability scanning actively probes systems for weaknesses, rather than reading public databases.
whyNot.E: White box testing describes a tester who has full knowledge of the target, not a way of gathering public data.

337.why: A packet sniffer passively captures network traffic without sending packets to targets, so it is the least likely tool to be detected by an IDS (Intrusion Detection System).

whyNot.A: A vulnerability scanner actively sends many probes, which generates noise and is easily detected.
whyNot.B: An offline password cracker works on already obtained hashes and gathers no information about the network.
whyNot.D: Banner grabbing connects to services to read their banners, which creates log entries and can be detected.

338.why: Documenting and securely storing captured evidence first serves to preserve the data, keeping it intact and unaltered so it remains usable in the investigation.

whyNot.A: Chain of custody is maintained by recording who handled the evidence, which is a result of documentation rather than the first purpose of storing it.
whyNot.C: A legal hold is a legal instruction to retain information and is not obtained by storing evidence.
whyNot.D: Recovering data later is a possible use of stored evidence, not the first reason for securing it.

339.why: A new account with UID (user identifier) 0 gives root-level access and is a backdoor, and the netstat command shows active network connections that reveal whether the attacker is still connected.

whyNot.A: A logic bomb runs malicious code when a condition is met, which does not describe adding a hidden root account.
whyNot.C: A keylogger captures keystrokes and does not modify the password file to create a new account.
whyNot.E: Tracert (trace route) shows the path packets take to a destination and does not show active connections on the host.
whyNot.F: Ping only tests whether a host responds and cannot show whether an attacker is currently connected.

340.why: Transference shifts the risk to a third party, here a provider that manages and insures the email and collaboration service.

whyNot.B: Acceptance means knowingly tolerating the risk without changing it, which is not what moving to an insured provider does.
whyNot.C: Mitigation reduces the likelihood or impact of the risk through controls, rather than shifting it to another party.
whyNot.D: Deterrence discourages attackers from acting and does not move the financial or operational risk to a third party.

341.why: The keyed answer is a keylogger, which records keystrokes and sends the captured data out over the network, producing the kind of traffic shown in the capture.

whyNot.B: Ransomware encrypts files and demands payment, and it would not typically send captured user input.
whyNot.C: A logic bomb waits for a trigger condition and does not generally produce this kind of ongoing network traffic.
whyNot.D: Adware displays unwanted advertisements and does not typically transmit captured keystroke data.

343.why: A Faraday cage blocks RF (radio frequency) signals, so an attacker cannot use a wireless device to reach into the air-gapped, locked server rack.

whyNot.B: Smart cards control who can authenticate at a door and do not stop radio signals from reaching the equipment.
whyNot.C: Infrared detection senses heat or motion and does not block RF (radio frequency) signals.
whyNot.D: Alarms only notify staff after an event and cannot prevent the wireless attack.

344.why: A stream cipher encrypts data one bit or byte at a time using a shared secret key, which makes it a symmetric algorithm.

whyNot.A: A hash function creates a fixed-length digest for integrity and is not an encryption cipher.
whyNot.B: Elliptic curve cryptography is an asymmetric method and is not a stream cipher.
whyNot.D: Public key cryptography uses key pairs and is asymmetric, so it is not a stream cipher.

345.why: A differential backup captures all changes since the last full backup, so restoring needs only the full backup plus the latest differential, which is faster than chaining many incremental backups.

whyNot.A: A full backup is slow to create and large, so it is not the answer the question's backup-efficiency framing intends.

whyNot.D: A proxy server relays network traffic and is not a method of gathering usernames or obtaining passwords through social engineering.

whyNot.F: MTTF (Mean Time To Failure) measures time until failure and is not changed by a faster replacement.

whyNot.E: Smart cards authenticate authorized users and do not detect trespassers.

370.why: Pivoting is using one compromised host as a foothold to reach other systems or networks, which matches moving from the poisoned server to one outside the original network.

whyNot.A: A backdoor is a hidden access method into a system and does not describe moving from one host to another.
whyNot.C: Persistence is maintaining access over time, such as after a reboot, and is not about reaching other hosts.
whyNot.D: A logic bomb is malicious code triggered by a condition and is not a method of lateral movement.

whyNot.B: A shared key is symmetric and secures only the RADIUS (Remote Authentication Dial-In User Service) client-server link, so it is not the asymmetric pair the key expects.
whyNot.C: Elliptic curve is a type of algorithm, not a required key component for this requirement.
whyNot.D: MD5 (Message Digest 5) is a weak hash function and does not encrypt credentials.

whyNot.C: RPO (Recovery Point Objective) defines acceptable data loss in time and is not an input to ALE (Annualized Loss Expectancy).
whyNot.E: RTO (Recovery Time Objective) defines acceptable downtime and is not an input to ALE (Annualized Loss Expectancy).

whyNot.D: A tabletop exercise rehearses response procedures with a scenario and does not apply historical findings from an actual breach.

whyNot.E: A red team exercise is a broad adversary simulation and does not describe the next step after enumeration.

402.keyDoubt: B. After enumeration, the next step is scanning for vulnerabilities, and an engagement with no prior knowledge is black-box rather than gray-box.

403.why: The decision between internal and third-party key management depends on weighing costs, risks, and benefits, so the company should use the results of a risk benefit analysis to decide.

whyNot.A: Choosing the current internal system only because it is reliable skips weighing its costs and risks against alternatives.
whyNot.B: Choosing a third party only to reduce operating costs ignores security and risk considerations that matter for key custody.
whyNot.D: A software solution with key escrow is one possible option, but picking it is premature without first analyzing risks and benefits.

404.why: Dual key pairs separate duties: one pair encrypts and decrypts for confidentiality, while the other signs data digitally, providing non-repudiation because the signing key is held only by its owner.

whyNot.B: Extended validation is a certificate vetting level for identity assurance and is not a function of a second key pair.
whyNot.C: Encrypting twice with two keys does not double non-repudiation, which comes from digital signatures with a private key.
whyNot.D: Separating keys by internal and external use does not address confidentiality or non-repudiation as distinct functions.

405.why: For globally traveling sales staff, password complexity protects accounts exposed to varied networks, and group-based access control assigns permissions consistently by role without per-user management.

whyNot.A: Time-of-day restrictions would block staff working across many time zones while traveling.
whyNot.C: Location-based authentication would repeatedly block or burden users who legitimately travel all over the world.
whyNot.E: A standard naming convention helps account administration but is not a security practice tied to traveling users.

406.why: An email DLP (Data Loss Prevention) control stops PII (Personally Identifiable Information) from being leaked through email, and a spam filter blocks many whaling phishing messages aimed at executives.

whyNot.A: A reverse proxy protects and load-balances inbound access to web servers and does not stop email leaks or phishing.
whyNot.D: A host-based firewall filters network connections on a single machine and does not inspect email content or block phishing messages.
whyNot.E: A HIDS (Host-based Intrusion Detection System) only detects suspicious host activity and does not prevent data leaks or whaling emails.

407.why: EAP-TLS (Extensible Authentication Protocol-Transport Layer Security) uses mutual certificate authentication, so both the authentication server and every client endpoint device must be issued digital certificates.

whyNot.A: TACACS+ (Terminal Access Controller Access-Control System Plus) is mainly used for network device administration and is not required for EAP-TLS (Extensible Authentication Protocol-Transport Layer Security).
whyNot.B: Federation between authentication servers is not needed, because EAP-TLS (Extensible Authentication Protocol-Transport Layer Security) works with a single authentication server and a shared certificate authority.
whyNot.C: TOTP (Time-based One-Time Password) is a separate one-time code method, and EAP-TLS (Extensible Authentication Protocol-Transport Layer Security) relies on certificates instead.

408.why: The data owner is the senior person accountable for the data and decides its classification and sensitivity level, so the IS (Information Systems) manager should consult the owner.

whyNot.A: A data steward manages data quality and governance policies day to day but does not decide the classification level.
whyNot.B: A data custodian implements and maintains the technical controls that protect the data, following the classification the owner has chosen.
whyNot.C: A user only accesses data as permitted and has no authority to decide how sensitive the data is.

409.why: A certificate is built from a public key submitted to a certificate authority, which signs it. The private key must stay secret, so the safe step is giving only the public key to the internal CA (Certificate Authority).

whyNot.A: A private key must never be given to anyone, and a public CA (Certificate Authority) would not sign a certificate for an internal website anyway.
whyNot.B: Giving only the public key to the internal CA (Certificate Authority) is the correct, safe practice, so this option is arguably the best answer, even though the key names a different letter.
whyNot.C: A public CA (Certificate Authority) is not appropriate for an internal website, because it would not validate or issue certificates for private internal names.
whyNot.E: Sending the whole public and private key pair exposes the private key, which breaks the basic rule of public key cryptography.
whyNot.F: Sending the key pair to a public CA (Certificate Authority) exposes the private key and uses the wrong type of CA for an internal site.

409.keyDoubt: B. A certificate request needs only the public key, and the private key must never leave the server, so giving the private key to the internal CA (Certificate Authority) is unsafe.

410.why: A corrective control acts after an incident to limit damage and restore normal operations, and a guard's post-incident review feeds lessons learned back into recovery and improvements.

whyNot.A: Detective controls, such as CCTV (Closed-Circuit Television) recordings, support reviewing events after the fact, so this fits a guard's review better than the key does.
whyNot.B: Preventive controls stop an incident before it happens, so they cannot be the basis of a review after an incident.
whyNot.D: Deterrent controls only discourage attackers through visible warnings, such as signs, and do not support reviewing an incident.

410.keyDoubt: A. A guard reviewing recorded evidence after an incident is a detective control, because it identifies what happened rather than correcting it.

411.why: OCSP (Online Certificate Status Protocol) stapling has the server attach a signed, timestamped revocation status to its certificate, so clients can detect and reject revoked certificates used in MITM (Man-in-the-Middle) attacks.

whyNot.A: A captive portal is a web page requiring login or acceptance before network access, and it does not check certificate revocation.
whyNot.C: OIDs (Object Identifiers) are numeric labels naming certificate fields and policies, and they do nothing to detect revoked certificates.
whyNot.D: Key escrow stores copies of private keys for recovery and does not tell clients whether a certificate has been revoked.
whyNot.E: An EV (Extended Validation) certificate proves stronger organization identity checks but does not by itself make clients check for revocation.

412.why: A fuzzer sends malformed and unexpected input to an application, which helps reveal whether SQL (Structured Query Language) injection and other input handling flaws remain after hardening.

whyNot.A: The tracert tool only shows the network hops to a destination and tests nothing about application input handling.
