whyNot.C: The nslookup tool queries DNS (Domain Name System) records and cannot test an application for SQL (Structured Query Language) injection.
whyNot.D: Nmap discovers hosts, open ports, and services, but it does not probe web application input for SQL (Structured Query Language) injection.
whyNot.E: The netcat tool opens raw network connections for manual testing and does not systematically test for SQL (Structured Query Language) injection.

413.why: Requiring applications to be digitally signed means code that was not vetted and signed is rejected, which limits the unsigned software that jailbreaking normally allows users to install.

whyNot.A: Mobile antivirus can detect some malware but does not stop users from jailbreaking a BYOD (Bring Your Own Device) phone.
whyNot.B: Blocking third-party application stores reduces risky app sources, but it does not enforce trust in the code itself the way digital signing does.
whyNot.C: Building a custom ROM (Read-Only Memory) image is impractical for personally owned BYOD (Bring Your Own Device) phones and is not a standard best practice.

414.why: Vishing is voice phishing, so its key difference from phishing is that it is carried out over telephony services such as phone calls or VoIP (Voice over Internet Protocol).

whyNot.A: Identity theft can be the goal of both vishing and phishing, so it does not distinguish them.
whyNot.B: Both vishing and phishing may use target knowledge, so needing it is not a key difference between them.
whyNot.D: Phishing being a social engineering category is true, but vishing is also social engineering, so it does not separate the two.

415.why: A passive scan observes traffic without sending probes, so it can identify vulnerabilities on a fragile legacy system without risking a crash or disruption.

whyNot.B: An aggressive scan sends many probes quickly and could crash or disrupt a fragile legacy system.
whyNot.C: A credentialed scan needs valid logins and actively queries the host, so it is not the safest first step on an unknown legacy system.
whyNot.D: An intrusive scan can exploit or change the target, which risks outages on a legacy system.

416.why: The embedded web server on a printer or MFD (Multifunction Device) is network-reachable and is often left with default credentials or weak settings, making it a common compromise vector.

whyNot.B: The print spooler queues jobs and is not normally exposed as the main remote management interface of the device.
whyNot.C: The network interface only carries traffic and is not by itself the vulnerable management component.
whyNot.D: The LCD (Liquid Crystal Display) control panel needs physical access, so it is less likely to be a remote vector.

417.why: A packet capture containing authentication data, such as password hashes or credentials, is attacked with a password cracker to recover the original passwords offline.

whyNot.B: A vulnerability scanner probes live systems for weaknesses and does not analyze captured traffic for credentials.
whyNot.C: A DLP (Data Loss Prevention) scanner is a defensive tool that detects sensitive data leaving an organization, not an attacker's tool.
whyNot.D: A fuzzer sends malformed input to applications to cause failures and does not process captured packets for credentials.

418.why: A new listening port after installing unknown software suggests a RAT (Remote Access Trojan), which opens a backdoor for an attacker to control the system remotely.

whyNot.B: A worm spreads itself across the network on its own, and a new listening port is not its main sign.
whyNot.C: Ransomware encrypts files and shows a ransom demand, and it does not typically open a listening port.
whyNot.D: A bot connects out to a command server to receive instructions, rather than mainly opening a listening port, which fits a RAT (Remote Access Trojan) better.

419.why: Based on the key, the exploit code writes new content over an existing document on the mail server, which is replacing a document rather than only reading it or touching a cookie.

whyNot.A: Replacing a cookie would involve session data held by a browser, and the key does not describe the code that way.
whyNot.B: Stealing a document would involve reading or copying the file out, not writing new content over it.
whyNot.D: Deleting a cookie would involve removing session data from a browser, which does not match overwriting a server document.

420.why: MDM (Mobile Device Management) software centrally enforces remote wipe, geolocation, patch reporting, screen locks, passcodes, and encryption on smartphones and laptops, covering every listed requirement.

whyNot.B: Group policies mainly apply to domain-joined Windows machines and lack remote wipe and geolocation for smartphones.
whyNot.C: Full device encryption protects stored data only and does not provide remote wipe, geolocation, patch reporting, or screen locks.
whyNot.D: Removing administrative rights limits what users can change but does not provide remote wipe, geolocation, or patch reporting.

421.why: The iexplore.exe entry shows a different MD5 (Message Digest 5) hash for the source and target, meaning the file was altered. A file integrity check should be reviewed to detect such tampering.

whyNot.A: A WAF (Web Application Firewall) protects web servers from application attacks and does not explain a modified executable on an endpoint.
whyNot.C: DEP (Data Execution Prevention) blocks code running from memory areas and does not show changed MD5 (Message Digest 5) hashes of files.
whyNot.D: Removable media control restricts USB (Universal Serial Bus) devices, and the USB.exe entry shows matching hashes, so the mismatch points elsewhere.

422.why: The key treats policy clarity (A) and awareness training topics (F) as the lessons learned outputs, since both address the human weaknesses the attacker exploited. Both are administrative rather than logical controls.

whyNot.B: Improved log correlation and alerting is a useful logical control, but the key does not select it.
whyNot.C: Raw data from IDS/IPS (Intrusion Detection System/Intrusion Prevention System) tools is evidence for the timeline, not a recommendation to improve the security posture.
whyNot.D: NAC (Network Access Control) improvements for AAA (Authentication, Authorization, and Accounting) are logical controls, but the key does not select them.
whyNot.E: A phase-by-phase activity summary documents what happened but does not propose logical control improvements.

422.keyDoubt: B and D, because the team was tasked to address logical (technical) controls, and A and F are administrative controls, while B (log correlation, alerting) and D (NAC (Network Access Control) improving AAA (Authentication, Authorization, and Accounting)) are logical.

423.why: MFA (multifactor authentication) needs different factor types. A proximity card is something you have, a fingerprint is something you are, and a PIN (Personal Identification Number) is something you know.

whyNot.B: Fingerprint and voice recognition are both inherence (something you are) factors, so only two distinct factor types are used.
whyNot.C: A smart card, a user PKI (Public Key Infrastructure) certificate, and a privileged user certificate are all possession-type factors, so they are not unique factors.
whyNot.D: Voice recognition is inherence, but a smart card and a proximity card are both possession factors, so only two distinct factor types are used.

424.why: Error handling means returning generic failure messages. Telling the user the password does not match the username and is not the required 12 characters leaks information that helps an attacker.

whyNot.A: Input validation checks that submitted data is safe and well formed, but the problem here is what the application reveals in its response.
whyNot.C: Obfuscation makes code hard to read or reverse engineer and does not control the messages shown to users.
whyNot.D: Data exposure is the general risk outcome, whereas the secure coding technique that prevents this verbose message is error handling.

425.why: A sandbox isolates an untested application from the host, preventing it from escalating privileges or reaching the host system if it turns out to be malicious or flawed.

whyNot.A: Sandboxes deliberately restrict access to host resources and storage rather than granting full access.
whyNot.B: A sandbox is meant to contain the application, and relying on host antivirus and firewall instead of protection is not its purpose.
whyNot.D: Sandboxing adds isolation overhead and does not increase processing speed or help real-time logging.

426.why: Unauthorized software, such as malware or a hosted illicit service, can consume disk space while also generating or attracting extra inbound internet traffic, which fits both symptoms.

whyNot.A: Misconfigured devices could cause traffic problems but do not explain disk space being consumed on several servers.
whyNot.B: Log and event anomalies could fill disks, but nothing in the scenario points to logging as the cause rather than unwanted software.
whyNot.C: Authentication issues involve failed or abused logins and do not by themselves explain disk exhaustion.

427.why: A CPU (Central Processing Unit) pinned at 100 percent is resource exhaustion, and if it is left unresolved the server can become unresponsive to legitimate users, which is a DoS (Denial of Service) condition.

whyNot.A: A MITM (Man-in-the-Middle) attack intercepts traffic and is not caused by high CPU utilization.
whyNot.C: DLL (Dynamic Link Library) injection is an attack technique and not a consequence of an antivirus program using too much CPU (Central Processing Unit).
whyNot.D: A buffer overflow is a coding flaw exploited by attackers and is not caused by sustained CPU load.

428.why: MD5 (Message Digest 5) is a hashing algorithm that produces a fixed-length digest, so comparing digests validates data integrity, although MD5 is considered weak against collisions.

whyNot.A: CBC (Cipher Block Chaining) is a block cipher mode of operation for confidentiality, not an integrity check.
whyNot.B: Blowfish is a symmetric encryption cipher that provides confidentiality rather than integrity validation.
whyNot.D: RSA (Rivest-Shamir-Adleman) is an asymmetric algorithm used for encryption and key exchange, not a hash for integrity.

429.why: Untrusted host errors on a web-based VPN (Virtual Private Network) typically mean the server's digital certificate has expired or is otherwise invalid, so the browser refuses to trust it.

whyNot.B: A browser lacking SSL (Secure Sockets Layer) support would fail to negotiate a secure connection and would not give an untrusted host warning.
whyNot.C: A locked account would produce an authentication failure message, not an untrusted host error.
whyNot.D: Reaching the VPN (Virtual Private Network) seat license limit would deny a session after login and would not raise a certificate trust error.

430.why: IaaS (Infrastructure as a Service) gives the customer control of the operating systems, storage, and deployed applications, so it offers the most control of the common cloud service models.

whyNot.B: PaaS (Platform as a Service) means the provider manages the operating system and runtime, so the customer has less control.
whyNot.C: SaaS (Software as a Service) gives the customer the least control because the provider manages the whole application stack.
whyNot.D: Virtualization is an underlying technology, not a cloud service model.

431.why: For a network incident, traffic captures and logs show what communicated with what and when, so they are the most likely evidence to identify and scope the incident.

whyNot.A: A volatile memory capture preserves host runtime state and is more useful for investigating a compromised system than for network activity.
whyNot.C: Screenshots capture only what was displayed at one moment and give little detail about network activity.
whyNot.D: A system image capture preserves a host's disk contents and is better for host forensics than for a network incident.

432.why: The output indicates a socket to a non-standard port, and nc (netcat) with a target address and the -p option for port 9856 is the command that would establish such a connection.

whyNot.A: The traceroute command maps hops to a destination and does not create a socket on a chosen port.
whyNot.B: The ping command sends ICMP (Internet Control Message Protocol) echo requests and does not create a TCP (Transmission Control Protocol) socket on a chosen port.
whyNot.D: The pskill command terminates a process and does not establish a network connection.

433.why: The key selects FTP (File Transfer Protocol) over a non-standard port plus certificate-based authentication, but the option that actually protects sensitive files in transit is not FTP.

whyNot.A: TOTP (Time-based One-Time Password) is a one-time code for interactive logins and does not suit an unattended scheduled script or secure file transfer.
whyNot.B: SCP (Secure Copy Protocol) is a strong choice that encrypts file transfers, but the key does not select it.
whyNot.D: SRTP (Secure Real-time Transport Protocol) secures voice and video media streams and not file uploads.
whyNot.F: SNMPv3 (Simple Network Management Protocol version 3) manages and monitors network devices and is not a file transfer method.

433.keyDoubt: B and E, because FTP (File Transfer Protocol) is unencrypted even on a non-standard port, whereas SCP (Secure Copy Protocol) encrypts the transfer and certificate-based authentication suits an unattended scheduled script.

434.why: A hardened host can still show many non-compliant results if the scan policy includes plugins that do not apply to it, and the report can contain false positives.

whyNot.A: Privileged-user certificates would give the scan more access and accuracy, so they would not explain many non-compliant findings.
whyNot.C: An incorrect audit file could cause mismatches, but the key selects non-applicable plugins and false positives instead.
whyNot.E: The scenario says the host is known to be hardened, and compromise is not suggested by non-compliance findings alone.

435.why: Sandboxing isolates a third-party application so an unknown vulnerability cannot easily affect the rest of the system, reducing risk without needing a patch.

whyNot.B: Encryption protects data confidentiality and does not stop an unknown vulnerability from being exploited.
whyNot.C: Code signing verifies the publisher and integrity of code but does not make vulnerable code safe.
whyNot.D: Fuzzing finds vulnerabilities through malformed input, but it needs access to test the software and does not reduce risk from an unknown flaw in production.

436.why: Setting the OS (Operating System) default TTL (Time To Live) to 1 means packets expire after the first router hop, so traffic cannot be routed beyond the local gateway, regardless of firewall misconfiguration.

whyNot.B: NAT (Network Address Translation) hides internal addresses but is not a security control and can be bypassed by port forwarding or misconfiguration.
whyNot.C: A router ACL (Access Control List) is a network control that could itself be misconfigured, which the requirement rules out.
whyNot.D: Protected ports on a switch isolate ports from each other at Layer 2 and do not stop routing to the Internet.

437.why: Separation of duties splits critical tasks such as creating, modifying, and approving payroll data among different people, so no single role can complete the whole process alone.

whyNot.A: Least privilege limits each role to the minimum access it needs, but one role could still legitimately hold create, modify, and approve rights.
whyNot.B: Job rotation moves staff between roles periodically to detect fraud, but it does not stop one role from holding conflicting permissions.
whyNot.C: Background checks screen people before hiring and do not restrict what access a job role has.

438.why: Pivoting means using a compromised host as a foothold to attack other systems deeper inside the network that the attacker could not reach directly.

whyNot.A: Escalating privilege means gaining higher permissions on a system, not using one host to reach other hosts.
whyNot.B: Becoming persistent means maintaining access across reboots or logins, not launching attacks onward from the compromised host.
whyNot.C: Fingerprinting identifies operating systems and services on a target, and it is reconnaissance rather than attacking through a compromised host.

439.why: The failure happens only after hours and works the next morning, which points to a time-of-day restriction in the account's logon hours policy.

whyNot.A: An expired password would block the login at every hour of the day until it was reset, not only in the evening.
whyNot.B: Missing remote access rights would block the employee all the time, yet the login worked in the morning.
whyNot.D: A locked-out account stays locked until unlocked or a timer expires, and it would not repeatedly fail only at night.

440.why: A router connects subnets and gateways, so a host from an unassigned network sending to the wrong gateway means the router interface has the wrong subnet configured, and placing the correct subnet fixes it.

whyNot.A: A firewall ACL (Access Control List) filters traffic but does not correct which subnet an interface serves or which gateway hosts use.
whyNot.C: Changing an access port to a trunk port carries multiple VLANs (Virtual Local Area Networks) and does not fix a subnet or gateway mismatch.
whyNot.D: A proxy handles application requests for clients and does not define the subnet or gateway that hosts on the network use.

441.why: Many consumer devices such as WiFi (Wireless Fidelity) baby monitors ship with default usernames and passwords, and attackers easily find and use these when owners never change them.

whyNot.A: Outdated antivirus does not apply to a baby monitor, which typically cannot run antivirus software at all.
whyNot.B: WiFi (Wireless Fidelity) signal strength affects range and reliability and does not give an intruder authenticated access to the device.
whyNot.C: Social engineering manipulates people, and nothing in the scenario suggests the intruder tricked the parents into granting access.

442.why: A certificate with a SAN (Subject Alternative Name) extension lists multiple host names, so one X.509 certificate can be installed on three servers and still match each host name the client checks.

whyNot.A: A wildcard certificate covers many subdomains of one domain, but it fails if the three servers use different domains, and the SAN (Subject Alternative Name) list is more precise.
whyNot.B: An EV (Extended Validation) certificate proves stronger organizational identity and does not by itself cover multiple host names.
whyNot.C: Certificate chaining links a certificate to its issuing certificate authorities and does not make one certificate match several host names.

443.why: MTTR (Mean Time To Repair) is the average time needed to restore a failed system to its operational state.

whyNot.A: MTBF (Mean Time Between Failures) measures the average time a system runs between failures, not how long repair takes.
whyNot.C: RTO (Recovery Time Objective) is the target maximum downtime, which is a goal rather than the measured time to restore a system.
whyNot.D: RPO (Recovery Point Objective) defines the maximum acceptable data loss measured in time, not the time to restore a system.

444.why: A penetration test actively attempts to exploit the flaw, which confirms whether the vulnerability exists and shows how much harm an attacker could actually cause.

whyNot.B: A vulnerability scan can detect that the flaw is present but does not exploit it, so it cannot show the extent of potential harm.
whyNot.C: Active reconnaissance gathers information about targets, such as open ports, and does not demonstrate the business impact of a specific flaw.
whyNot.D: A patching assessment report shows patch status, not whether the flaw is exploitable or how far an attacker could get.

445.why: TACACS+ (Terminal Access Controller Access-Control System Plus) and RADIUS (Remote Authentication Dial-In User Service) are centralized authentication, authorization, and accounting protocols commonly used to manage logins to network devices from one server.

whyNot.B: CHAP (Challenge-Handshake Authentication Protocol) is an authentication method for a single link and does not provide centralized management of many device accounts.
whyNot.C: LDAP (Lightweight Directory Access Protocol) is a directory access protocol and is not the usual protocol for network device administrator authentication and accounting.
whyNot.E: MSCHAPv2 (Microsoft Challenge-Handshake Authentication Protocol version 2) is an authentication method that can run inside other protocols and is not a centralized management solution itself.

446.why: An active/passive configuration keeps a standby system ready to take over when the active one fails, which improves availability.

whyNot.A: Confidentiality protects data from unauthorized disclosure, and a standby system does not change who can read the data.
whyNot.B: Integrity protects data from unauthorized modification, and a failover pair does not by itself prevent changes.
whyNot.D: Non-repudiation prevents someone from denying an action, typically through digital signatures and logs, and is unrelated to failover design.

447.why: A PIN (Personal Identification Number) is something you know, so combining it with a smart card, which is something you have, adds a second authentication factor.

whyNot.A: A token is also something you have, so adding it to a smart card gives two items of the same factor type rather than a new factor.
whyNot.B: A proximity badge is also something you have, so it duplicates the factor type already provided by the smart card.
whyNot.C: A physical key is also something you have, so it adds no new factor beyond the smart card.

448.why: RADIUS (Remote Authentication Dial-In User Service) federation lets the network authenticate devices and users through a central server using IEEE 802.1X before the captive portal login appears.

whyNot.A: L2TP (Layer 2 Tunneling Protocol) is a tunneling protocol, and MAC (Media Access Control) filtering is easily spoofed and does not authenticate mobile devices properly.
whyNot.B: EAP-TTLS (Extensible Authentication Protocol Tunneled Transport Layer Security) is an authentication method, but it needs a RADIUS (Remote Authentication Dial-In User Service) back end and does not provide the federation described.
whyNot.C: WPA2-CCMP (Wi-Fi Protected Access 2 with Counter Mode with Cipher Block Chaining Message Authentication Code Protocol) with a PSK (Pre-Shared Key) uses one shared password and does not authenticate individual devices.

449.why: Rainbow tables are precomputed lists of hashes and their plaintext values that attackers look up to recover passwords quickly.

whyNot.A: Iptables is a Linux firewall tool that filters packets and does not crack passwords.
whyNot.B: NAT (Network Address Translation) tables map private addresses to public ones and have nothing to do with password hashes.
whyNot.D: ARP (Address Resolution Protocol) tables map IP (Internet Protocol) addresses to hardware addresses and do not store password hashes.

450.why: Unlabeled media of unknown origin may carry malware, so the most immediate safe action is to confiscate it and dispose of it securely under company policy without ever inserting it into a computer.

whyNot.B: Inserting unknown media into a computer risks executing malware and infecting the system, and returning it leaves the threat in place.
whyNot.C: Holding unclaimed media for a month keeps a possible threat on site and delays the immediate response that is needed.
whyNot.D: Copying the disc requires inserting it into a computer, which risks infection, and returning the original leaves the hazard on the desk.

451.why: Blocking personal email on corporate systems and prohibiting social media access reduce the channels through which employees receive phishing messages and leak proprietary information publicly.

whyNot.A: An additional firewall filters network traffic by rules and does not stop users from opening malicious links or PDFs (Portable Document Format files) in email.
whyNot.B: A redundant email server improves availability of email and does nothing to reduce phishing risk.
whyNot.D: Updating X.509 certificates on the email server maintains encryption and server identity, but it does not stop malicious messages from reaching users.
whyNot.F: Reviewing access violations on the file server may help investigate the leak, but it does not reduce the phishing messages employees receive.

452.why: After evidence is gathered and secured, eradication and recovery come next: removing malware and restoring systems returns the business to normal operation and limits ongoing impact.

whyNot.A: Identifying the attacking host is attribution work and does not restore business operations or reduce downtime.
whyNot.B: The IRP (Incident Response Plan) should already have been initiated before evidence was collected, so it is not the next step.
whyNot.C: Lessons learned is the final phase of incident response and happens after eradication and recovery.

453.why: Joe broke the company's policy requiring a VPN (Virtual Private Network) on untrusted public wireless, so a policy violation exposed the emails to interception.

whyNot.B: Social engineering manipulates a person through deception, and no attacker tricked Joe in this scenario.
whyNot.C: An insider threat implies malicious intent or deliberate harm, while Joe acted carelessly without malice.
whyNot.D: A zero-day attack exploits an unknown software vulnerability, and intercepting unencrypted traffic on open wireless needs no such flaw.

454.why: A mission-essential function is a business function whose outage causes losses in revenue, referrals, or reputation, which is what the BIA (Business Impact Analysis) is examining here.

whyNot.B: A single point of failure is a component whose loss stops a service, not the analysis of business losses from an outage.
whyNot.C: Backup and restoration plans are recovery measures, not the identification of what causes business loss when unavailable.
whyNot.D: Identification of critical systems maps functions to technology, whereas the question describes the business functions and their loss impact.

455.why: Shredding physically destroys the storage media, so data cannot be recovered and the drive cannot be reused, which meets the stated requirement.

whyNot.B: Wiping erases the data but leaves the drive intact and reusable.
whyNot.C: Low-level formatting resets the drive structure, and the drive remains usable afterward.
whyNot.D: Repartitioning only changes the partition table, leaving data recoverable and the drive reusable.
whyNot.E: Overwriting replaces the stored data but the drive remains functional and reusable.

456.why: Chain of custody begins by documenting receipt of the evidence, so updating the evidence log is the first step before any handling or analysis.

whyNot.A: Making a forensic copy is a handling step that should only occur after custody has been recorded in the evidence log.
whyNot.B: Creating a hash verifies integrity but comes after the evidence receipt is documented in the log.
whyNot.C: Recovering data is analysis work that happens after custody is established and a forensic copy exists.

457.why: The Identification phase of the IRP (Incident Response Plan) is where the responder confirms an incident and determines its scope, such as affected PCs, accounts, and who has been notified.

whyNot.A: Recovery restores systems to normal operation after eradication, and nothing is being restored yet.
whyNot.B: Eradication removes the threat from systems, but the manager is still gathering facts about scope.
whyNot.C: Containment isolates affected systems to stop spread, but the manager has only collected facts so far.

458.why: A cloud-based disaster recovery site is geographically distributed, scales automatically, and is always available with the least staff effort, which fits the always-operational and low man-hours goal.

whyNot.A: A hot site is ready to run but requires staff to maintain duplicate hardware and data, using more man hours than a cloud site.
whyNot.B: A warm site needs staff time and effort to bring systems fully online, so it is not always operational.
whyNot.C: A cold site has only space and power with no equipment, so it takes the longest and most labor to activate.

459.why: A trust model, such as cross-certification between the two PKIs (Public Key Infrastructures), lets each organization's certificates be trusted by the other and prevents certificate errors.

whyNot.B: OCSP (Online Certificate Status Protocol) stapling delivers revocation status quickly but does not establish trust between separate PKIs.
whyNot.C: An intermediate CA (Certificate Authority) sits inside one hierarchy and does not by itself make two independent PKIs trust each other.
whyNot.D: Key escrow stores copies of keys for recovery and has nothing to do with cross-organization certificate trust.

460.why: Pass-the-hash abuses captured NTLM (New Technology LAN Manager) password hashes to authenticate, so disabling NTLM removes the mechanism and minimizes the risk.

whyNot.A: CHAP (Challenge-Handshake Authentication Protocol) is not the Windows hash-based authentication being abused in pass-the-hash.
whyNot.C: Enabling Kerberos alone leaves NTLM available as a fallback, so pass-the-hash attacks remain possible.
whyNot.D: PAP (Password Authentication Protocol) is unrelated to Windows NTLM hashes, so disabling it does not stop pass-the-hash.

461.why: A vulnerability scanner reports software versions, running services, supported encryption algorithms, and permission settings while checking systems for known weaknesses.

whyNot.B: A protocol analyzer captures and inspects network packets and does not report installed software versions or permission settings.
whyNot.C: A network mapper discovers hosts and open ports but does not assess permission settings or supported encryption algorithms in depth.
whyNot.D: A web inspector examines page code and requests in a browser and does not produce an assessment of services and permissions.

462.why: ALE (Annualized Loss Expectancy) equals SLE (Single Loss Expectancy) times ARO (Annualized Rate of Occurrence). With an ARO of 5, an SLE of $500 gives an ALE of $2500, which does not exceed the $2500 protection cost.

whyNot.B: An SLE (Single Loss Expectancy) of $1000 gives an ALE (Annualized Loss Expectancy) of $5000, which exceeds the $2500 cost, so buying protection is justified.
whyNot.C: An SLE (Single Loss Expectancy) of $2000 gives an ALE (Annualized Loss Expectancy) of $10000, far above the $2500 cost, so protection is justified.
whyNot.D: An SLE (Single Loss Expectancy) of $2500 gives an ALE (Annualized Loss Expectancy) of $12500, far above the cost, so protection is justified.

463.why: System sprawl is the uncontrolled growth of VMs (Virtual Machines) across business units, which consumes cluster resources and leaves unmanaged systems, matching the audit finding.

whyNot.A: A buffer overflow is a memory-handling flaw in software code and does not describe a cluster running out of compute resources.
whyNot.B: End-of-life systems are no longer supported by the vendor, which is unrelated to running low on cluster resources.
whyNot.D: Weak configuration refers to insecure settings, not to excess VMs (Virtual Machines) exhausting cluster capacity.

464.why: A passive scan observes traffic and system information without sending probes, so it identifies vulnerabilities without impacting the web application or its data.

whyNot.A: An aggressive scan sends intensive probes and tests that can disrupt the system or alter its data.
whyNot.C: A non-credentialed scan lacks login access but still actively probes the target, so it can still impact the system.
whyNot.D: A compliance scan checks configuration against a standard and does not describe avoiding impact on the system.

465.why: A symmetric algorithm uses one shared key and is fast, making it the right choice for encrypting large amounts of data between two parties.

whyNot.B: A hash function is one-way and cannot be reversed, so the receiver could never decrypt the data.
whyNot.C: A digital signature proves authenticity and integrity but does not provide confidentiality for bulk data.
whyNot.D: Obfuscation only makes data harder to read and is not strong encryption, so it does not protect transmitted data.

466.why: A policy requiring employees to have badges rekeyed annually is a written rule governing behavior and procedure, which makes it an administrative control.

whyNot.A: A physical control is the tangible barrier itself, such as a lock or badge reader, while this item is a policy about it.
whyNot.B: A corrective control repairs damage after an incident, and an annual rekeying policy is not a response to an event.
whyNot.C: A technical control is enforced by technology such as software or hardware logic, and this item is a policy decision.

467.why: Hard-coding the full path to each DLL (Dynamic Link Library) in the application stops Windows from searching other directories, so an attacker cannot plant a malicious DLL earlier in the search order.

whyNot.A: Setting each application's DLL individually is vague and does not control the search path an attacker exploits to load a malicious DLL (Dynamic Link Library).
whyNot.C: Disabling DLL (Dynamic Link Library) access from the Windows registry would break applications and does not address the search-order weakness that hijacking abuses.
whyNot.D: Renaming DLLs (Dynamic Link Libraries) is security through obscurity; an attacker can still place a malicious file with the expected name or discover the new name.

468.why: Input validation checks and rejects malformed or unexpected data before the application processes it, which directly prevents attacks that arrive through web form fields.

whyNot.B: A proxy server filters and forwards traffic but does not validate the content of form fields inside the application's own processing logic.
whyNot.C: Stress testing measures how an application performs under heavy load and does not stop malformed data from being accepted.
whyNot.D: Encoding transforms output so it is rendered safely, but it does not reject malformed input the way input validation does before processing.

469.why: Recovery is the incident response phase where systems are restored to normal operation, including rebuilding from original media and returning user data to the machine.

whyNot.B: Eradication removes the threat, such as malware or attacker access, from the environment; restoring user files comes after that work is already done.
whyNot.C: Containment limits the spread or impact of an incident by isolating affected systems, which happens before rebuilding and restoring data.
whyNot.D: Identification is the phase of detecting and confirming that an incident occurred, which takes place well before restoring a workstation.

470.why: A keylogger records keystrokes, which explains a file holding URLs, usernames, passwords, and text from documents the user was typing or editing.

whyNot.B: A rootkit hides malicious processes and files with privileged access, but its main purpose is concealment rather than capturing typed text into a file.
whyNot.C: A bot (compromised host in a botnet) takes remote commands for tasks like attacks or spam, and does not typically log typed credentials and document text.
whyNot.D: A RAT (Remote Access Trojan) gives an attacker remote control, but the file of captured typed content is characteristic of keylogging functionality.

471.why: During an active exfiltration, the team must first identify the source of the connection, which is the identification step of incident response, before choosing containment or eradication actions.

whyNot.B: Eradication and recovery come after the incident is understood and contained, so performing them first would skip scoping and could destroy evidence.
whyNot.C: Disconnecting the server is containment, which follows identification of the connection; acting blindly could lose volatile evidence and miss other compromised systems.
whyNot.D: Formatting and restoring the server destroys forensic evidence and skips identification, containment, and proper eradication, so it is not the next step.

472.why: Banner grabbing retrieves service banners that reveal software names and version numbers, which an intruder can then match against known exploits during reconnaissance.

whyNot.B: Port scanning finds open ports and running services but does not by itself reliably reveal the specific software versions in use.
whyNot.C: Packet sniffing captures traffic passing on a network segment and is passive eavesdropping, not an inventory technique for software versions across the network.
whyNot.D: Virus scanning looks for malware on a system and does not enumerate software versions on remote hosts for exploit research.

473.why: Accounting, the last part of AAA (Authentication, Authorization, and Accounting), tracks and records user actions through logging and auditing so activity can be reviewed later.

whyNot.B: Authorization determines which resources and actions an authenticated user is permitted to use, not the recording of what the user did.
whyNot.C: Authentication verifies a user's claimed identity using credentials such as passwords or tokens and does not record the user's later actions.
whyNot.D: Identification is the user claiming an identity, such as providing a username, and does not track or log subsequent activity.

474.why: Rogue system detection discovers unauthorized or unknown hosts that appear on the network, which matches a scanner built to identify new host systems.

whyNot.A: A vulnerability scanner looks for known weaknesses on hosts it already targets, rather than focusing on detecting new unknown hosts joining the network.
whyNot.B: A NIDS (Network-based Intrusion Detection System) inspects traffic for malicious patterns and does not primarily inventory newly connected host systems.
whyNot.D: A configuration compliance scanner checks whether known systems match a security baseline and does not find new or unauthorized hosts.

475.why: Risk acceptance means knowingly taking on a risk without added controls, which fits a decision that safeguards are not cost effective for a known vulnerability.

whyNot.A: Transference shifts the risk to another party, such as through insurance or outsourcing, and nothing in the scenario moves the risk elsewhere.
whyNot.B: Avoidance eliminates the risk by stopping the risky activity altogether, whereas the CIO (Chief Information Officer) is continuing operations with the vulnerability present.
whyNot.C: Mitigation reduces likelihood or impact by implementing safeguards, which the CIO (Chief Information Officer) explicitly decided not to do.

476.why: Adware displays unwanted advertisements and installs things like new search toolbars, and it commonly causes browser slowness, crashes, and high memory use.

whyNot.A: A man-in-the-browser attack intercepts and alters web transactions such as banking, and typically stays hidden rather than adding visible toolbars and slowing the browser.
whyNot.B: A spoofer impersonates another identity, address, or system, and does not explain the toolbar and resource-consumption symptoms described.
whyNot.C: Spyware secretly gathers user information and usually tries to remain unnoticed, so it would not typically add a visible new search toolbar.

477.why: XORing bytes with a fixed value like 0xFF is trivially reversible without a secret key, so it only obscures the data rather than securing it, which is obfuscation.

whyNot.A: Hashing is a one-way function producing a fixed-length digest, whereas an XOR (exclusive OR) with a constant can be directly reversed to recover the original data.
whyNot.B: Key exchange securely establishes a shared secret between parties, such as with Diffie-Hellman, and a fixed XOR operation does not do that.
whyNot.C: Encryption relies on a secret key and a strong algorithm; a fixed XOR (exclusive OR) with 0xFF has no key secrecy and offers no real confidentiality.

478.why: A mantrap is an access control vestibule with two interlocking doors that allows only one person through at a time, preventing tailgating at the main entrance.

whyNot.A: A Faraday cage blocks electromagnetic signals to prevent wireless eavesdropping or emanation leaks and does not control physical entry by people.
whyNot.B: An air gap isolates a network from other networks physically, which does not stop unauthorized people from walking into the building's entrance.
whyNot.D: Bollards stop vehicles from ramming into a building and do not prevent unauthorized people from entering on foot.

479.why: Retina scans and fingerprint scans are biometric factors, which authenticate users based on physical characteristics, the 'something you are' factor.

whyNot.A: A MAC (Media Access Control) address table maps device addresses to switch ports and is not a user authentication method based on physical traits.
whyNot.D: Two-factor authentication combines two different factor types and is not itself a physical characteristic; it could include non-biometric factors only.
whyNot.E: CAPTCHA (Completely Automated Public Turing test to tell Computers and Humans Apart) distinguishes humans from bots and does not authenticate a user by physical characteristics.
whyNot.F: A password string is something you know, a knowledge factor, and not a physical characteristic of the user.

480.why: A tabletop exercise is a discussion-based simulation where staff walk through a hypothetical disruption and then update the disaster recovery plan and documentation.

whyNot.A: A BIA (Business Impact Analysis) identifies critical functions and the impact of their loss, and is not a group simulation of an interruption.
whyNot.B: Continuity of operations is the broader planning goal of keeping essential functions running, not the specific act of simulating an event in a meeting.
whyNot.D: Order of restoration defines the sequence in which systems are brought back online and is not a simulated exercise by the team.

481.why: Certificate 1 includes the intermediate Geotrust CA in its path while Certificate 2 lacks it, so certificate chaining, which installs the full chain on the server, lets browsers validate trust.

whyNot.A: Both portals already use the same wildcard certificate for *company.com, so a wildcard certificate does not address the missing intermediate CA (Certificate Authority) in one path.
whyNot.C: A trust model describes how trust is structured among certificate authorities in general and is not a specific fix for a server missing its intermediate certificate.
whyNot.D: An EV (Extended Validation) certificate changes the identity vetting level and does not fix a missing intermediate certificate causing browser trust errors.

482.why: Federation (a trust relationship between separate identity systems) lets two organizations keep independent domains while still accepting each other's authentication, so users can reach resources across both companies.

whyNot.A: Attestation (proving a system's state or identity) does not establish cross-domain authentication between two separate organizations.
whyNot.C: SSO (Single Sign-On) reduces repeated logins within one trust realm and does not by itself join two unmergeable domains.
whyNot.D: Kerberos is an authentication protocol that operates within or between Kerberos realms and is not the cross-organization trust method asked about.

483.why: Locality-based load balancing sends each request to the server closest to the client, which reduces latency and speeds up application performance while still spreading traffic across multiple redundant servers.

whyNot.A: Round-robin rotates through servers in order without considering distance or speed, so it does not specifically accelerate network performance.
whyNot.B: Weighted balancing favors servers by assigned capacity, which helps uneven hardware but does not target network proximity or performance.
whyNot.C: Least connection sends traffic to the server with the fewest active sessions, which balances load rather than shortening the network path.

484.why: SSO (Single Sign-On) lets users authenticate once and access multiple internal resources, replacing three separate sets of credentials with one and making the process less complex.

whyNot.A: Transitive trust extends trust between domains automatically but does not reduce the number of credentials a user must manage.
whyNot.C: Federation links identities across separate organizations, which is more than needed for internal resources within one company.
whyNot.D: A secure token is a single authentication factor or device and does not consolidate multiple credential sets by itself.

485.why: Modifying a computer's ARP (Address Resolution Protocol) cache with false address mappings is ARP spoofing (also called poisoning), where the attacker impersonates another host on the local network.

whyNot.A: A replay attack resends previously captured valid traffic and does not alter an ARP (Address Resolution Protocol) cache.
whyNot.C: DNS (Domain Name System) poisoning corrupts name-to-address records in DNS caches, not ARP (Address Resolution Protocol) caches.
whyNot.D: A client-side attack exploits software on the user's device, such as a browser, and does not describe forging ARP (Address Resolution Protocol) entries.

486.why: After containment (isolating the system) and eradication (terminating the malicious process), the incident response process moves to recovery, which includes restoring lost data from a backup.

whyNot.B: Wiping the system is a heavier eradication step and is not the next stage once the malicious process has already been stopped.
whyNot.C: Documenting lessons learned is the final phase of incident response and happens after recovery is complete.
whyNot.D: Determining the scope of impact belongs to the earlier identification and analysis phase, which precedes containment and eradication.

487.why: An intrusive scan actively tests vulnerabilities and can crash services, and a non-credentialed scan probes from outside without login access, so an intrusive non-credentialed scan is most likely to cause an outage.

whyNot.A: A non-intrusive credentialed scan only reads configuration with valid logins and does not exploit anything, so it rarely disrupts systems.
whyNot.B: A non-intrusive non-credentialed scan only observes exposed services without exploiting them, so it is unlikely to crash a system.
whyNot.C: An intrusive credentialed scan can cause disruption, but credentials let it gather information directly, making it less likely than an uncredentialed intrusive scan to trigger crashes.

488.why: A captive portal can collect and log guest email addresses on an open network, and WPA2 Enterprise (Wi-Fi Protected Access 2 with 802.1X authentication) is the most secure of the listed methods for staff.

whyNot.A: WPS (Wi-Fi Protected Setup) uses a weak PIN-based process and is not the most secure staff authentication method.
whyNot.B: A captive portal is not a secure staff authentication method, and WPA (Wi-Fi Protected Access) on guests conflicts with the open network requirement.
whyNot.C: WEP (Wired Equivalent Privacy) is broken and insecure, and an open guest network should not use it.

489.why: A NIPS (Network-based Intrusion Prevention System) can block worm traffic inline, including exploits of unknown zero-day vulnerabilities through anomaly detection, and stops spreading across the network.

whyNot.A: A host-based firewall protects only the individual host it runs on and would need configuration on every system to stop the worm.
whyNot.B: Enterprise patch management fixes known vulnerabilities such as the old SMB (Server Message Block) flaw but cannot protect against future zero-day vulnerabilities.
whyNot.D: Application blacklisting blocks known bad programs and does not stop network-based exploitation or unknown zero-day attacks.
whyNot.E: File integrity checking detects changes to files after the fact and neither eradicates the worm nor prevents zero-day exploitation.

490.why: Sandboxing runs applications in an isolated environment with limited access, so software only gets the OS (Operating System) resources it needs and cannot affect the wider system.

whyNot.A: A staging environment is a pre-production copy used for testing releases and does not restrict which OS (Operating System) access an application gets.
whyNot.C: A secure baseline is a standard hardened configuration and does not isolate an application's access to the OS (Operating System).
whyNot.D: A trusted OS (Operating System) enforces strong access controls system-wide, but it is not a deployment concept for exposing only required access to an application.

491.why: A procedure is a detailed, step-by-step set of instructions for carrying out a specific task, whereas a policy states high-level management direction.

whyNot.A: A high-level statement of the company's position on a topic describes a policy, not a procedure.
whyNot.B: Setting a minimum expected baseline of behavior describes a standard or baseline, not a procedure.
whyNot.D: Describing adverse actions for violations describes the enforcement or sanctions portion of a policy, not a procedure.

492.why: The log comes from Ann's own desktop and the user's access was verified, so a host-based firewall on that machine is the most likely control blocking the application's traffic.

whyNot.A: A WAF (Web Application Firewall) protects web servers and would not appear in a log from Ann's desktop.
whyNot.B: DLP (Data Loss Prevention) blocks sensitive data leaving the organization and does not typically prevent a user from reaching an application.
whyNot.D: A UTM (Unified Threat Management) device is a network appliance, so its blocks would be logged on that device and not on Ann's desktop.
whyNot.E: A network-based firewall logs on the network device, not in a log file from Ann's own system.

493.why: A gray box penetration test gives the tester partial knowledge, such as password hashes, before testing begins, which sits between no knowledge and full knowledge.

whyNot.A: A black box test gives the tester no prior information, so the tester would not have password hashes in advance.
whyNot.C: A credentialed test uses valid login accounts, which is more than only password hashes and describes access level rather than knowledge level.
whyNot.D: A white box test gives the tester full knowledge of the environment, which is more than access to password hashes alone.

494.why: Insiders already have legitimate access and detailed knowledge of systems, data, and security controls, so they can cause the most damage to an organization.

whyNot.A: Competitors are external and usually lack detailed internal knowledge unless they recruit an insider.
whyNot.C: Hacktivists are motivated by ideology and typically attack from outside with limited knowledge of internal systems.
whyNot.D: Script kiddies use prebuilt tools with little technical understanding, so they have the least knowledge and capability.

495.why: A CRL (Certificate Revocation List) published by the certificate authority lists revoked certificates, so checking it shows whether a certificate is still valid or has been revoked.

whyNot.A: PKI (Public Key Infrastructure) is the overall framework for managing certificates and is not itself the way to check one certificate's validity.
whyNot.C: A CSR (Certificate Signing Request) is submitted to request a new certificate and does not verify an existing one.
whyNot.D: IPSec (Internet Protocol Security) encrypts and authenticates network traffic and does not check certificate validity.

496.why: Time-of-day restrictions limit logins to the hours personnel are on the clock, reducing exposure of trade secrets by blocking access outside scheduled work times.

whyNot.B: Password complexity strengthens passwords but does not limit when temporary and contract personnel can access network resources.
whyNot.C: A random key generator strategy creates unpredictable keys and does not restrict access to working hours.
whyNot.D: Account expiration disables accounts on a set end date, but it does not stop access outside daily working hours.
whyNot.E: A password lockout policy blocks accounts after failed attempts and does not control when users may log in.

497.why: Cache memory sits closest to the CPU (Central Processing Unit) and loses its contents the instant power is removed, so it is the most volatile item in the order of volatility.

whyNot.A: An SSD (Solid State Drive) is non-volatile storage and keeps its data without power.
whyNot.B: A paging file lives on disk and persists across power loss, so it is less volatile than cache memory.
whyNot.C: RAM (Random Access Memory) is volatile, but data in CPU cache is lost even faster, so RAM is not the most volatile.

498.why: Missing files combined with a demand for payment to restore them is the signature of ransomware, which encrypts or locks data and extorts the victim.

whyNot.B: A keylogger records keystrokes to steal information and does not remove files or demand payment.
whyNot.C: A buffer overflow is a memory-corruption exploit and does not itself produce a ransom demand.
whyNot.D: A rootkit hides malicious activity at a deep level of the OS (Operating System) and is not tied to extortion for file recovery.

499.why: A dummy account that exists only to attract attackers is a honeypot (or honeytoken) decoy, and failed logins against it reveal attacker activity.

whyNot.A: RBAC (Role-Based Access Control) assigns permissions by job role and does not lure attackers.
whyNot.C: Rule-based access control applies fixed rules such as time-of-day limits and is not a decoy.
whyNot.D: A password cracker is an attacker tool for recovering passwords and is not a defensive decoy.

500.why: The message header arrives but the encrypted attachment does not, which suggests Ann cannot be authenticated or validated to receive or decrypt the protected content.

whyNot.A: Unencrypted credentials would expose passwords but would not block delivery of an attachment.
whyNot.C: A weak cipher suite reduces encryption strength and does not stop a file from being delivered.
whyNot.D: Permission issues affect file or folder access on a system, which is less likely to block an email attachment in transit.

501.why: MAC (Mandatory Access Control) enforces access by comparing data classification labels, such as Confidential or Secret, against user clearance levels set by the system.

whyNot.A: DAC (Discretionary Access Control) lets the data owner grant access and does not depend on classification labels.
whyNot.C: RBAC (Role-Based Access Control) grants access by job role, not by data classification label.
whyNot.D: Rule-based access control applies administrator-defined rules such as time or location limits and does not use classification labels.

502.why: A vulnerability scanner checks configuration against a baseline, so a disabled firewall on workstations is a typical misconfiguration finding.

whyNot.C: Browser homepages are cosmetic preferences and not a security misconfiguration a scanner would flag.
whyNot.D: Default administrator credentials are a classic misconfiguration finding, so this is arguably correct even though the key omits it.
whyNot.E: Checking for updates once a day is an acceptable setting and not a security misconfiguration.

502.keyDoubt: D: Default administrator credentials on networking hardware are a textbook scanner misconfiguration finding, while SSH (Secure Shell) being enabled on servers is normal and not inherently a misconfiguration.

503.why: WSUS (Windows Server Update Services) distributes operating system and Microsoft application patches, so a client that has not reported in 30 days has not pulled the latest updates.

whyNot.A: ACL (Access Control List) firewall rules are not delivered or tracked through WSUS (Windows Server Update Services).
whyNot.B: GPO (Group Policy Object) settings come from Active Directory, not from the WSUS (Windows Server Update Services) status report.
whyNot.C: Antivirus definitions are normally updated by the antivirus vendor's own management console, not by WSUS (Windows Server Update Services).

504.why: A script scheduled in Task Scheduler on a database server that performs a harmful action at a set time or condition is a logic bomb, malicious code triggered by an event.

whyNot.A: Ransomware encrypts files and demands payment, which a scheduled trigger script alone does not indicate.
whyNot.B: A backdoor provides hidden remote access and is not defined by a scheduled trigger.
whyNot.D: A Trojan disguises itself as legitimate software to get installed, which is not what a scheduled script shows.

505.why: Redundancy across all network devices and services removes single points of failure, such as the 1 Gbps (gigabit per second) router and the session-limited application, so DoS (Denial of Service) load does not take everything down.

whyNot.A: Web servers with a load balancer help the application but leave the router as a single point of failure.
whyNot.B: Raising the router to 10 Gbps (gigabits per second) only moves the bottleneck and leaves the application session limit unaddressed.
whyNot.C: A firewall cannot prevent all attacks, and a DoS (Denial of Service) flood can still overwhelm it.

506.why: A SYN (Synchronize) flood leaves many half-open TCP (Transmission Control Protocol) connections waiting for the final ACK (Acknowledgment), which exhausts the server's connection table and memory.

whyNot.A: SYN (Synchronize) packets are small, and the damage comes from half-open state rather than bandwidth consumption.
whyNot.B: The firewall is not the main target, and the attack works by exhausting server connection resources.
whyNot.C: SYN (Synchronize) floods do not involve fragmented packets that must be reassembled.

507.why: Rapid elasticity lets a cloud or virtual environment quickly add resources under heavy load, which absorbs traffic spikes and mitigates DoS (Denial of Service) conditions.

whyNot.A: Elasticity scales resources and does not protect the confidentiality of data.
whyNot.B: A VM (Virtual Machine) escape is a hypervisor vulnerability issue, which elasticity does not address.
whyNot.C: Redundancy comes from replication and failover design, not from elasticity, which only adds or removes capacity.

508.why: Login proceeds by identification (claiming an identity), then authentication (proving it), and finally authorization (granting permissions).

whyNot.B: Authorization cannot come before authentication because permissions require a verified identity.
whyNot.C: Authentication cannot come before identification because there must be a claimed identity to verify.
whyNot.D: This repeats option C and has the same wrong order, with authentication before identification.
whyNot.E: Authorization comes last, since access rights are granted only after identity is proven.

509.why: Full disk encryption protects data at rest only when the drive is offline, so someone with local console access to the running server can read and copy the decrypted data.

whyNot.B: Full disk encryption specifically protects against stolen physical drives, so this risk is mitigated.
whyNot.C: Remote access is limited by the Read Only share permission for accounting-svc, and the question stresses local risk.
whyNot.D: The share permissions are restrictive, with only a single service account having Read Only access, so excess exposure is not the main risk.

510.why: A Faraday cage blocks electromagnetic signals from leaving the premises, which stops outsiders from capturing wireless transmissions of credit card data.

whyNot.A: An air gap isolates a network physically and would not allow a wireless network to function.
whyNot.B: Infrared detection senses heat or light and does not stop radio signals from leaking.
whyNot.D: Protected distribution secures physical cabling, not wireless transmissions.

511.why: The caller falsely claims to be an employee to gain access to an account, which is impersonation, a social engineering technique that exploits trust.

whyNot.A: Phishing uses deceptive email or messages at scale, and this is a direct phone call.
whyNot.B: Shoulder surfing means watching someone enter sensitive information in person.
whyNot.D: Dumpster diving means searching discarded materials for sensitive information.

512.why: S/MIME (Secure/Multipurpose Internet Mail Extensions) encrypts the message body end to end, and SMTPS (Simple Mail Transfer Protocol Secure) encrypts mail in transit, so a sniffer would see only ciphertext instead of plain text.

whyNot.A: Secure IMAP (Internet Message Access Protocol) also protects mail retrieval in transit, but it was not one of the two keyed answers and does not protect messages sent between servers.
whyNot.B: DNSSEC (Domain Name System Security Extensions) signs DNS records to prove authenticity but does not encrypt email content, so sniffed emails would still be readable.
whyNot.E: HTTPS (Hypertext Transfer Protocol Secure) protects web traffic, not email protocols such as SMTP (Simple Mail Transfer Protocol), so it would not stop email sniffing.

513.why: SSO (Single Sign-On) lets a user authenticate once and use the same credentials across multiple applications without keeping separate credentials synchronized.

whyNot.A: MFA (Multifactor Authentication) adds extra proof of identity but does not let one set of credentials work across multiple applications.
whyNot.C: Biometrics verify identity using physical traits, but they do not provide one credential set shared across applications.
whyNot.D: PKI (Public Key Infrastructure) manages certificates and keys, and it is not designed to let users reuse one username and password across applications.
whyNot.E: Federation shares identity across separate organizations or domains, which is broader than the single-organization need for one set of credentials.

514.why: Unclaimed printouts containing PII (Personally Identifiable Information) and medical data are a privacy policy violation, so reporting it to the human resources manager lets the owner fix the process and address the exposure.

whyNot.A: Flipping documents face down only hides them briefly and leaves sensitive PII (Personally Identifiable Information) exposed and unaddressed.
whyNot.B: Shredding the documents destroys them without reporting the violation, and it does not fix the underlying policy failure.
whyNot.C: Adding a PII (Personally Identifiable Information) cover sheet and returning the documents to the printer leaves the sensitive data unattended and exposed.

515.why: Gait analysis measures how a person walks, which is a behavior, so it falls under the something you do authentication factor.

whyNot.A: Somewhere you are relies on location, such as GPS (Global Positioning System) or network address, not on how a person moves.
whyNot.B: Something you are covers static physical traits such as fingerprints or retina patterns, while gait is a learned behavior.
whyNot.D: Something you know covers secrets such as passwords or PINs (Personal Identification Numbers), which gait does not involve.

516.why: SLE (Single Loss Expectancy) is asset value times exposure factor, and it relates to ALE (Annualized Loss Expectancy) and ARO (Annualized Rate of Occurrence) because ALE equals SLE times ARO, so SLE equals ALE divided by ARO.

whyNot.A: ROI (Return on Investment) measures the financial benefit of a purchase and is not used to calculate SLE (Single Loss Expectancy).
whyNot.D: MTBF (Mean Time Between Failures) measures reliability of repairable systems and is not an input to SLE (Single Loss Expectancy).
whyNot.E: MTTF (Mean Time To Failure) measures expected lifespan of non-repairable items and is not an input to SLE (Single Loss Expectancy).
whyNot.F: TCO (Total Cost of Ownership) measures lifetime cost of an asset and is not used to calculate SLE (Single Loss Expectancy).

517.why: Using an internal Stratum 0 NTP (Network Time Protocol) source keeps time synchronization inside the organization, so it avoids exposure to spoofed or tampered external time sources.

whyNot.A: External Stratum 0 NTP (Network Time Protocol) sources are not reachable over the network, and relying on external sources exposes the servers to spoofing.
whyNot.C: External Stratum 1 NTP (Network Time Protocol) servers depend on outside sources over the internet, which is less secure than an internal reference clock.
whyNot.D: External Stratum 1 NTP (Network Time Protocol) servers depend on outside sources over the internet, which is less secure than an internal reference clock.

518.why: Both parties must first agree on which encryption method, such as the algorithm, they will use before they can exchange keys or send encrypted messages.

whyNot.A: Exchanging the encryption key comes after the parties agree on the method, because the key format depends on the chosen algorithm.
whyNot.B: Digital signatures provide authenticity and non-repudiation, and they are not required before symmetric encryption can begin.
whyNot.D: Digital certificates support asymmetric encryption and identity validation, and they are not required to start symmetric encryption.

519.why: A digitally signed email proves who sent it and that it was not altered, so the sender cannot later deny sending it, which is non-repudiation.

whyNot.A: Logging into a workstation and accessing file shares shows authentication and access, and it does not prove who sent or approved an action.
whyNot.B: Using another user's credentials is impersonation, which undermines non-repudiation because actions cannot be tied to the true person.
whyNot.D: Making unauthorized registry changes is a policy violation and does not provide proof of origin or prevent denial.

520.why: Dates of birth, addresses, and phone numbers are PII (Personally Identifiable Information), so the officer should consult the PII portion of the policy to decide whether a breach occurred.

whyNot.A: Public data is intended for open release, and client dates of birth and addresses are not public information.
whyNot.B: Private is a general classification label and does not specifically address personal identifiers that trigger breach rules.
whyNot.C: PHI (Protected Health Information) covers health-related data, and the folder contained no medical details.

521.why: DHE (Diffie-Hellman Ephemeral) is an asymmetric key exchange that generates a new, separate key pair for each session, which provides forward secrecy.

whyNot.A: RSA (Rivest-Shamir-Adleman) uses a long-term key pair and does not generate a new separate key every time it runs.
whyNot.B: DSA (Digital Signature Algorithm) creates digital signatures using a long-term key pair, not a fresh key each time.
whyNot.D: HMAC (Hash-based Message Authentication Code) is a symmetric integrity function that uses a shared key and does not generate new keys.
whyNot.E: PBKDF2 (Password-Based Key Derivation Function 2) stretches passwords into keys and is not an asymmetric function.

522.why: A strong password is something you know and a fingerprint is something you are, so together they combine two different authentication factors.

whyNot.A: A hardware token and a smart card are both something you have, so they are the same factor.
whyNot.B: Voice recognition and a retina scan are both something you are, so they are the same factor.
whyNot.D: A PIN (Personal Identification Number) and security questions are both something you know, so they are the same factor.

523.why: A bot is a compromised device controlled remotely to join a botnet, and a hacked surveillance camera sending attack traffic at a website matches a botnet used for a DDoS (Distributed Denial of Service) attack.

whyNot.B: A RAT (Remote Access Trojan) gives an attacker remote control of a device, but the scenario describes coordinated attack traffic typical of a bot.
whyNot.C: A Trojan is malware disguised as legitimate software, and that does not specifically explain participation in an attack on another website.
whyNot.D: A backdoor is a hidden way to bypass authentication, and it does not itself describe the camera sending attack traffic.

524.why: Tailgating means following an authorized person through a badge-controlled door without presenting a badge, which directly bypasses badge readers.

whyNot.A: Phishing uses deceptive messages to steal information and does not defeat a physical badge reader.
whyNot.B: A man-in-the-middle attack intercepts network communication and does not help someone get through a physical door.
whyNot.D: A watering hole attack compromises websites visited by targets and is not a physical entry method.
whyNot.E: Shoulder surfing observes someone entering secrets, and it does not by itself get a person past a badge reader.

525.why: An imaging solution deploys the same hardened, approved configuration to every PC, which creates a consistent security baseline across all 500 machines.

whyNot.A: Faster deployment is an efficiency benefit, not a security benefit.
whyNot.C: Imaging does not reduce the number of vulnerabilities by itself, because the image can include vulnerable software unless it is patched.
whyNot.D: Decreased boot time is a performance benefit and has no direct security value.

526.why: IPSec (Internet Protocol Security) tunnel mode encrypts and encapsulates the entire original packet, including the header, which makes it the most secure choice for remote user VPN (Virtual Private Network) access.

whyNot.B: Transport mode protects only the payload and leaves the original IP (Internet Protocol) header visible, so it is less secure for remote access.
whyNot.C: AH (Authentication Header) provides integrity and authentication but no encryption, so the data would remain readable.
whyNot.D: ESP (Encapsulating Security Payload) alone does not specify tunnel encapsulation of the full packet, so it is less complete than tunnel mode.

527.why: A vendor-supplied patch fixes the flaw in the vulnerable OS (Operating System) versions. Removing the vulnerability itself is a corrective control, because it repairs the weakness after it was found.

whyNot.A: An antivirus definition update only improves malware signature detection and does not fix a vulnerability in the OS (Operating System) itself.
whyNot.B: User education is a preventive administrative measure and does not correct the unpatched OS (Operating System) weakness on the workstations.
whyNot.C: Server isolation is a compensating containment measure for servers, and it does not repair the vulnerable workstation OS (Operating System) versions.
whyNot.E: An IDS (Intrusion Detection System) only detects attacks and cannot remove the underlying vulnerability, so it is detective rather than corrective.

528.why: Querying the workstation's own hostname with dig sends a fresh lookup to the DNS (Domain Name System) server. A prompt, correct answer shows the server is responding normally and no longer overwhelmed by the DDoS (Distributed Denial of Service) attack.

whyNot.A: Looking up www.google.com may be answered from cache or forwarded externally, so it does not clearly prove the local DNS (Domain Name System) server is healthy after the DDoS (Distributed Denial of Service) attack.
whyNot.B: Running dig against an IP (Internet Protocol) address as the query name is not a valid forward lookup and would not test DNS (Domain Name System) resolution of a host.
whyNot.D: Running dig against an IP (Internet Protocol) address as the query name is not a proper lookup without a reverse option, so it does not verify DNS (Domain Name System) recovery.

529.why: TACACS+ (Terminal Access Controller Access-Control System Plus) authenticates over TCP (Transmission Control Protocol) port 49, and RADIUS (Remote Authentication Dial-In User Service) accounting uses UDP (User Datagram Protocol) port 1813.

whyNot.A: TCP (Transmission Control Protocol) 389 is LDAP (Lightweight Directory Access Protocol), not RADIUS (Remote Authentication Dial-In User Service) accounting.
whyNot.B: UDP (User Datagram Protocol) 1812 is the RADIUS (Remote Authentication Dial-In User Service) authentication port, not the accounting port.
whyNot.E: TCP (Transmission Control Protocol) 88 is Kerberos, not TACACS+ (Terminal Access Controller Access-Control System Plus), which uses TCP port 49.
whyNot.F: UDP (User Datagram Protocol) 636 is not a TACACS+ (Terminal Access Controller Access-Control System Plus) port, since LDAPS (Lightweight Directory Access Protocol over SSL) uses TCP 636.

530.why: The execute denials show application whitelisting is blocking the legitimate ERP (Enterprise Resource Planning) DLL (Dynamic Link Library) files. Whitelisting only those libraries restores function with minimal added risk and attack exposure.

whyNot.A: Updating the blacklist would block more items rather than allow the blocked ERP (Enterprise Resource Planning) DLL (Dynamic Link Library) files to run.
whyNot.B: Verifying DLL (Dynamic Link Library) file integrity checks for tampering but does not lift the execute permission denial caused by the application control policy.
whyNot.D: Adding users to the local administrators group grants excessive privilege and greatly increases attack exposure, violating least privilege.

531.why: An anomaly-based IDS (Intrusion Detection System) compares activity against a learned baseline and alerts on deviations, such as an unexpected spike in network traffic after working hours.

whyNot.B: Stateful describes tracking connection state, as in firewalls, and does not describe alerting on a traffic spike from baseline deviation.
whyNot.C: A host-based IDS (Intrusion Detection System) monitors activity on a single endpoint, whereas a network traffic spike points to network-level monitoring.
whyNot.D: A signature-based IDS (Intrusion Detection System) matches known attack patterns and would not alert on a general traffic volume increase with no known signature.
